pages.title: Safety before circuit theory: recognize the energy source
pages.text: Before a technician measures anything, the first question is not “What reading should I get?” It is “What can this source do if something goes wrong?”
pages.remember: The correct outcome is a documented safe decision, not a voltage reading.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Why the question matters

Electricity is useful because it transfers energy. The same energy can injure a person, heat a conductor, damage a component, start a fire, or produce an arc. A wall outlet, a charged capacitor, and an isolated battery-powered trainer are not interchangeable situations. Their available energy, grounding, fault behavior, and accessibility differ. Never infer that a circuit is harmless from its small physical size or from a “low-voltage” label.
Build a hazard picture

Identify the source, its voltage and maximum available current, whether it is isolated, its stored energy, what conductive parts can be touched, and how power is disconnected. Ask who is qualified and authorized to work on it. A benchtop supply with a current limit is a training control, not permission to defeat barriers or handle exposed mains conductors. The safest first move with unfamiliar equipment is to leave it de-energized and obtain appropriate instructions.
The first technician decision

Separate two questions: “Is the circuit performing normally?” and “Is it safe for me to examine?” Correct voltage is not a safety clearance. A powered supply can still have exposed conductors or stored energy. An equipment switch in OFF does not independently prove absence of voltage. Treat the hazard controls as a process rather than a single button.

worked.heading: Case conference · unknown power unit
worked.scenario: A metal-cased module has an unplugged cable, but you do not know whether it contains a capacitor bank. A coworker suggests opening it immediately.
steps: Recognize that unplugging removes one possible input but does not establish absence of stored energy.
Do not open or probe the unit. Identify the equipment instructions and authorized energy-isolation procedure.
If the procedure calls for verification of a de-energized state, that verification belongs to a qualified person using suitable equipment.
worked.conclusion: The correct outcome is a documented safe decision, not a voltage reading.

check.ask: A switched-off device may still be hazardous. What is the best explanation?
options: The warning labels are only decorative.
A switch position alone does not eliminate stored or alternate energy sources.
Current can flow only when a motor is running.
check.why: Isolation and verification require an authorized procedure; OFF is not sufficient proof.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Do not work on exposed energized electrical equipment for this course.

pages.title: Shock physiology, emergency response and first-aid boundaries
pages.text: A shock occurs when electric current passes through the body. The seriousness of an exposure depends on the current path, amount, duration, frequency and contact conditions—not merely on a supply label.
pages.remember: Safety of the rescuer and removal of exposure come before first aid.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Current through the body

Human tissues conduct to varying degrees. Skin resistance depends on condition and contact; wet or damaged skin often lowers resistance. Contact across the chest is particularly concerning because current can disrupt heart rhythm and breathing. Involuntary muscle contractions can prevent someone from releasing a conductor. Burns may occur at contact points or deeper within tissue. Do not memorize a single “safe current” threshold or attempt a human experiment.
Resistance is variable, so voltage alone cannot predict injury

Ohm’s law relates voltage, current and resistance in a simplified circuit (I = V/R). A human body is not a fixed resistor: contact area, moisture, duration, the path and changing tissue behavior all affect the result. Consequently, a calculation of estimated current through a person is not a safe substitute for isolating the hazard.
If a person is being shocked

Do not grab or touch someone still in contact with electrical energy. Call emergency services. If it can be done without entering the hazard, have an authorized person disconnect the source or use the appropriate emergency disconnect. Stay clear of fallen power lines, damaged equipment and any area that may remain energized. After the scene is safe, follow emergency dispatcher instructions and your level of CPR/AED training. Electrical injuries can require medical evaluation even without dramatic visible burns.

worked.heading: Scenario · someone is unable to release a conductor
worked.scenario: You see a coworker rigidly gripping an energized-looking apparatus. Another person moves to pull them away.
steps: Warn others away from contact; do not become another victim.
Call emergency services and identify the source and location.
Direct trained/authorized responders toward safe power isolation; do not improvise live rescue methods.
Once the scene is certified safe, provide only the aid you are trained and directed to provide.
worked.conclusion: Safety of the rescuer and removal of exposure come before first aid.

check.ask: What is the correct first response to someone still touching an energized conductor?
options: Grab their arm to interrupt the contact.
Pour water on the equipment.
Keep clear, summon emergency help and arrange safe isolation by authorized personnel.
check.why: Direct contact with a shocked person can create a second victim.

source.title: NIOSH / CDC: Electrical Safety in the Workplace
source.task: Connect the guidance on qualification and exposure control to the rescue scenario.

pages.title: Codes, protective devices and the hierarchy of controls
pages.text: Electrical safety has several layers: safe design, isolation, protective devices, work procedures and training. No single layer replaces the others.
pages.remember: Changing protective-device ratings to conceal a fault removes a safety layer.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Know which rulebook is being discussed

NFPA 70, the National Electrical Code (NEC), mainly addresses safe electrical installation. NFPA 70E addresses electrical safety-related work practices. OSHA requirements are enforceable workplace rules in their applicable jurisdictions. Their purposes overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A technician should use the currently applicable local code, employer procedure, and qualified supervision instead of inventing a clearance rule from memory.
Fuse and circuit-breaker fundamentals

Both interrupt excessive current under specified conditions. A fuse melts its element; a circuit breaker trips through a designed mechanism and may be reset once the underlying fault has been corrected. Current rating is only one selection parameter: voltage rating, interrupting capacity, time-current behavior and application also matter. Never bridge a fuse, up-rate it to stop nuisance blowing, or assume two physically matching fuses are equivalent.
Personal protective equipment is the last layer

PPE helps manage residual risk, but does not turn an unsafe task into a safe one. Prefer eliminating exposure, isolating energy and using engineered controls and approved procedures. Gloves, glasses and clothing must be chosen for the actual hazard and inspected before use; generic safety glasses do not substitute for arc-rated PPE where required.

worked.heading: Decision study · repeated fuse operation
worked.scenario: An instrument repeatedly opens a specified 500 mA time-delay fuse. A colleague proposes replacing it with a 2 A fast-acting fuse because it fits.
steps: Identify that repeated operation suggests a fault or overload requiring investigation.
Compare the proposed part’s current rating, time behavior, voltage and interrupt rating against the manufacturer specification.
Reject substitution; keep the equipment out of service until the cause is evaluated by an authorized person.
worked.conclusion: Changing protective-device ratings to conceal a fault removes a safety layer.

check.ask: Which statement correctly distinguishes NEC from safe-work procedures?
options: The NEC primarily concerns installation; safe-work rules also cover what workers do during service.
The NEC is a personal protective glove standard.
An NEC-compliant installation never needs lockout.
check.why: Installation rules do not replace hazardous-energy control.

source.title: OSHA: Electrical Safety-Related Work Practices
source.task: Identify where de-energization verification is assigned to a qualified person.

pages.title: Lockout, stored energy and verification
pages.text: “Off” is a description of a control position. “De-energized and safe for work” is a condition established by an authorized process.
pages.remember: Safe energy control is multi-source and verified.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: What lockout/tagout prevents

Unexpected energization, startup, or release of stored energy can injure people during service. Energy may be electrical, mechanical, pneumatic, hydraulic or gravitational. An energy-control program identifies sources, establishes isolation steps, applies locks/tags as applicable, neutralizes stored energy and verifies isolation before work. A tag warns; by itself it does not physically block energy in the way a properly installed lock can.
Isolation is different from a stop button

A stop button or touchscreen command is part of the control circuit; it may fail or be overridden. The authorized energy-isolating device must be identified and controlled according to the equipment-specific procedure. A charged capacitor can remain hazardous after external power is removed. Never assume residual energy is gone because a display has turned dark.
Verify without guessing

Qualified workers must verify the state in a manner appropriate to the equipment and procedure. For electrical testing this includes suitably rated instruments and applicable proving practices. An absence-of-voltage test is not a beginner DIY activity on mains or high-energy equipment. For this course, practice the recognition and ordering of the steps using photographs and written cases; do not implement lockout on workplace equipment without authorization and training.

worked.heading: Applied case · conveyor service
worked.scenario: A stopped conveyor has a padlocked main isolator, but a suspended load and compressed-air line remain connected.
steps: List the electrical, pneumatic and gravitational energy sources.
Explain that locking the main electrical disconnect did not neutralize other energy.
Describe the employer-specific need to restrain, isolate and verify each applicable energy source before service.
worked.conclusion: Safe energy control is multi-source and verified.

check.ask: Which step completes an appropriate authorized lockout process before maintenance?
options: Observe that the display is dark.
Ask someone whether the power is off.
Verify isolation and control of stored energy according to the procedure.
check.why: The indicator state is not proof that every energy source has been controlled.

source.title: OSHA: Application of Energy Control
source.task: Read the sections on stored energy and verification; explain their difference.

video.title: Lockout / Tagout — Electrical Safety Foundation International

visual.alt: Two US Navy electrical workers reviewing a lockout tag attached to an industrial control panel
visual.caption: Actual lockout/tagout review: locate the controlled equipment, physical tag and the qualified workers. A tag visible in a photograph does not by itself prove every energy source has been isolated.

pages.title: Field safety: fire, ladders and service vehicles
pages.text: Technician hazards are not limited to electric current. Fire, falls, sharp edges, batteries, tools and moving equipment demand their own controls.
pages.remember: Good fieldwork often begins with deciding not to start.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Fire response starts with an exit plan

Recognize the alarm, evacuate, and call emergency services according to workplace procedures. Only trained personnel should consider using an appropriate extinguisher on a small, contained fire with a clear exit route. Familiar U.S. classes include A for ordinary combustibles, B for flammable liquids, C for energized electrical equipment, D for combustible metals and K for cooking oils/fats. Class C addresses energized equipment; removing energy can change the applicable fuel hazard, but you should not approach the hazard to accomplish that yourself.
Ladders are selected, inspected and positioned

Check ladder condition, appropriate rating, stable support, footing, and nearby electrical hazards. Maintain safe climbing technique and do not carry bulky equipment in your hands while climbing. Avoid conductive ladders near electrical exposure. The right ladder setup depends on its type and manufacturer instructions, not a universal one-size-fits-all number.
Vehicles and tools need an inspection routine

Secure transported batteries, chemicals and equipment; maintain sight lines and safe loading. Before using power tools, check guards, cords, bits and the designated work area. Know where to find SDS information for chemical hazards. Do not bypass interlocks to finish a task quickly.

worked.heading: Hazard walk · site arrival
worked.scenario: You arrive to inspect a rooftop communications enclosure. There is a wet access area, a cracked ladder foot and a chemical container with a damaged label.
steps: Stop: there are already multiple non-electrical hazards.
Record and report each defect to the authorized site contact.
Do not climb, enter the equipment area or handle unidentified chemicals until controls and instructions are established.
worked.conclusion: Good fieldwork often begins with deciding not to start.

check.ask: What should you do with a ladder showing a damaged rail or foot?
options: Use it slowly because the task is brief.
Remove it from use and follow the equipment reporting procedure.
Let another person hold it as the sole remedy.
check.why: Defective access equipment should not be used.

source.title: NIOSH: Workplace Electrical Safety
source.task: Write down which field conditions affect your decision to proceed.

pages.title: Electrical matter: charge, current, voltage and power
pages.text: Understanding how electricity behaves makes safety decisions less mechanical. We start with physical quantities before formulas.
pages.remember: The current is 9 mA and dissipation is 81 mW in the ideal resistor model; the setup must still be inspected before power.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Charge and current

Charge is a property of matter, measured in coulombs (C). In conductors, moving charge produces current. Current, I, measures charge transfer per second: 1 A = 1 C/s. In a closed circuit, a source creates an electrical potential difference that can drive current through a conductive path. A broken path prevents steady conduction in the simple model, but a capacitor may still hold charge.
Voltage is energy per unit charge

Voltage, V, is a potential difference measured in volts. One volt means one joule of energy change per coulomb of charge. Resistance, R, measured in ohms (Ω), expresses opposition to current in a simple resistive model. Ohm’s law I = V/R relates them for an ohmic resistor; it does not describe every nonlinear or changing device at all times.
Power links calculations to heating

Electric power is the rate of energy conversion: P = VI, measured in watts. For a resistor, P = I²R = V²/R. A component rated for less dissipation than the expected operating power can overheat. Therefore a bench calculation is not just exam arithmetic: it is a predictor of whether the chosen part is appropriate.

worked.heading: Fully worked · resistor current and power
worked.scenario: An isolated, current-limited 9.0 V training source feeds a 1.0 kΩ resistor. Determine ideal current and resistor power.
steps: Convert 1.0 kΩ = 1,000 Ω.
Compare 81 mW with the resistor’s rated power and consider manufacturer derating, heat and actual setup.
worked.conclusion: The current is 9 mA and dissipation is 81 mW in the ideal resistor model; the setup must still be inspected before power.

check.ask: A 5 V source across a 1 kΩ resistor produces approximately what current?
options: 5 mA
5 A
200 mA

pages.title: A controlled first power-up: inspect, predict, limit, observe
pages.text: A technician should be able to describe an expected safe outcome *before* connecting power.
pages.remember: A wildly different reading demands investigation, not a new guess.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

paragraphs: Begin with a deliberately modest circuit

For a safe training exercise use a fully isolated, approved low-voltage trainer, not household wiring, exposed mains supplies, salvaged power equipment or unknown batteries. Keep the circuit de-energized while inspecting component values, polarity, exposed conductors, connectors, and possible shorts. Read the instrument manual; do not assume every supply behaves identically.
Predict the expected measurement

Draw a source, load and return. Compute expected current from the circuit model, check component power and voltage ratings and write down a stop threshold. If a regulated bench supply is approved for the setup, check that its voltage and current limits are suitable. Its “current limit” is a backup, not an excuse to omit inspections.
Observe the first indications

Connect according to the trainer procedure. Watch for unexpected current limiting, voltage collapse, heating, odor or other abnormal behavior. Stop and de-energize if reality contradicts the plan. Do not “see whether it settles down” when a circuit behaves unexpectedly. Record measured versus predicted values along with instrument settings.

worked.heading: Prediction before energization
worked.scenario: An isolated 3.3 V source is intended to drive a 1.5 kΩ resistor. What current should you expect?
steps: Write a prediction of about 2.2 mA, then confirm value, connections and approved supply limits before a supervised exercise.
worked.conclusion: A wildly different reading demands investigation, not a new guess.

check.ask: If a supposedly 2.2 mA trainer circuit abruptly enters current-limit mode, what is your next decision?
options: Raise the current limit until the warning stops.
De-energize, inspect connections and revise the hypothesis safely.
Hold the resistor to see if it gets hot.
check.why: Unexpected behavior is a stop-and-investigate signal.

source.title: Fluke: Multimeter Safety Guide
source.task: Identify which instrument checks belong before the first reading.

pages.title: Digital multimeters: ports, modes and common mistakes
pages.text: The selector position and lead jacks determine how a meter connects to the circuit. A meter set incorrectly can create a hazardous fault.
pages.remember: Correct the instrument configuration before connecting it.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

paragraphs: Voltage and resistance are different measurements

To measure a voltage difference on an approved training circuit, a properly configured voltmeter is connected across two points. To measure resistance or continuity, the circuit must be de-energized and handled according to the equipment procedure. The meter injects a small test current in resistance modes; it is not designed as a live-circuit voltage tool.
Current measurement changes the circuit

Most handheld meters measure current by inserting a low-resistance path in series through a dedicated fused input. Accidentally placing that current input across a source can short it. Therefore, before any voltage reading, inspect the lead connection (usually COM and V/Ω, per the actual model), function/range, ratings, lead insulation, and proper test practice. Do not make hazardous-voltage measurements without qualified training.
Never infer a safe state from a dead display

A missing reading may reflect a damaged meter, wrong settings, poor probe contact or incorrectly chosen reference point. Suitability and proof of operation are separate from the numeric value shown. Follow the applicable rated-instrument and verification procedure, especially for any absence-of-voltage testing.

worked.heading: Meter-jack error without touching equipment
worked.scenario: A meter has its red lead in the A current jack. You plan to measure voltage across a 3.3 V training rail.
steps: Do not place the leads on the source.
With power disconnected, follow the manual to move the lead to the designated voltage jack and choose the voltage function.
Inspect leads and instrument ratings and then follow the approved trainer procedure.
worked.conclusion: Correct the instrument configuration before connecting it.

check.ask: Why can leaving the red lead in the A jack be dangerous for a voltage check?
options: It measures higher resistance.
It increases the display font size.
The low-resistance current input can effectively short a voltage source.
check.why: Current and voltage input circuits are not interchangeable.

source.title: OSHA: Field Service Memo on Electrical Testing Equipment
source.task: Find OSHA’s warning about applying resistance modes to energized circuits.

pages.title: ESD: protecting CMOS without creating a shock hazard
pages.text: Electrostatic discharge (ESD) is not the same hazard as electrical shock. A discharge you cannot feel can still damage electronics.
pages.remember: Controlling one hazard never excuses increasing another.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

paragraphs: Why devices are vulnerable

Insulating materials can accumulate charge through contact and separation. If objects at different electrical potentials suddenly connect, a rapid discharge may occur. Semiconductor gates and junctions can be damaged immediately or weakened so that a device fails later—latent failure. An intact-looking PCB is not proof of undamaged silicon.
What an ESD-protected workstation does

An approved ESD-protected area uses tested dissipative surfaces, common-point grounding, appropriate packaging and trained handling. Wrist straps are part of a defined personnel-grounding program for exposed sensitive devices. The goal is to avoid dangerous potential differences at the device, not to “earth” everything indiscriminately. A wrist strap is never a substitute for electrical shock protection; do not wear one when contacting potentially hazardous energized equipment.
Separate equipment protection from personal protection

A dissipation mat helps protect a board; it does not make an energized power assembly safe to service. Disconnect or isolate energy under the applicable work procedure, ensure the workstation is authorized, then handle exposed components. Choose shipping/handling materials that meet the ESD program rather than tossing a bare board in ordinary plastic.

worked.heading: Two different hazards at one workbench
worked.scenario: A technician is about to handle an exposed CMOS module while a high-energy supply remains open and energized nearby. They reach for an ESD wrist strap.
steps: Recognize the separate shock and ESD hazards.
Stop the handling task; address hazardous exposed energized equipment through qualified isolation first.
Only at the approved de-energized ESD bench, use the designated tested grounding and handling system.
worked.conclusion: Controlling one hazard never excuses increasing another.

check.ask: What is the key benefit of an ESD-protected mat and common ground?
options: They reduce unwanted potential differences and discharges to sensitive devices.
They guarantee that every power circuit is safe to touch.
They eliminate the need for isolation and verification.
check.why: ESD control protects components; it does not grant electrical work authorization.

source.title: EOS/ESD Association: ESD Control Procedures
source.task: Explain the purpose of common-point grounding and the correct scope of wrist straps.

visual.caption: Real ESD work area: identify the mat, grounding lead, and exposed circuit board. The photograph shows equipment protection, not a certification that the workstation is safe for energized repair.

pages.title: The pre-power hazard log and a technician’s report
pages.text: Technical competence includes recording what you expected, what you observed, and why a decision was safe.
pages.remember: A disciplined stop can be an excellent technician result.
pages.sourceLesson: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

paragraphs: Make an inspection reproducible

A useful record identifies the device, source, intended connections, expected values, instrument model/function, power state, safety controls, and who authorized the setup. A vague entry such as “looks fine” does not permit the next technician to reproduce your conclusion. A precise entry such as “3.3 V isolated trainer, 1.5 kΩ resistor, prediction 2.2 mA; power disconnected for wiring check” conveys intent.
Describe uncertainty honestly

If you have not physically measured the circuit, write “predicted,” not “verified.” If you completed an online simulation, write “simulated.” If a lab was guided by a trainer, distinguish observed output from independent performance. Photos and written reports do not substitute for signed equipment permits or workplace energy-control records.
The stop rule is a technical result

If polarity is uncertain, a connector is warm, insulation is damaged, or current is implausible, stop. Document the anomaly and your hypothesis without inventing an explanation. Many real failures are prevented by stopping before the attempted measurement.

worked.heading: Worked report · abnormal current
worked.scenario: A training circuit predicted 2.2 mA. On approved energization, a supply immediately indicates current limiting.
steps: Record the prediction, supply settings, observation and time.
De-energize through the trainer’s normal procedure; do not increase the limit.
List plausible causes, including a short, incorrect part, reversed connection or mistaken expected load.
Choose the next de-energized inspection and keep the outcome marked “not yet verified.”
worked.conclusion: A disciplined stop can be an excellent technician result.

check.ask: Which note is acceptable after completing only a paper-based simulation?
options: Circuit proven physically safe under all conditions.
Predicted 2.2 mA in the model; physical setup and measurement not performed.
Instrument certified accurate without checking it.
check.why: Evidence labels must not exceed the work actually performed.

source.title: OSHA: Energy Control Verification
source.task: Explain why verification is distinct from the plan or the written log.

pages.title: Less visible hazards: RF transmitters and optical fiber
pages.text: A source can be hazardous without a familiar mains conductor: electromagnetic fields and optical systems each have their own exposure mechanisms.
pages.remember: A dark port is not a demonstrated safe optical port.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

paragraphs: Radio-frequency exposure is exposure-dependent

RF energy is electromagnetic radiation. Risk depends on frequency, field strength/power density, source geometry, antenna gain, duty cycle, location and duration. Maximum permissible exposure (MPE) frameworks provide frequency-dependent limits; there is no single universally safe distance. Never enter a controlled transmitter area based on the transmitter being “small” or because an antenna looks harmless.
Optical systems carry multiple hazards

A fiber can transmit radiation outside the visible spectrum; lack of a visible light spot does not prove absence of laser energy. Never stare into an active fiber connector or a port, and use rated inspection equipment under the appropriate procedure. Cut fiber shards are extremely fine and can puncture skin or eyes; manage scraps using appropriate containment and approved cleanup steps rather than bare hands.
Classify and escalate

In both RF and optical environments, technicians identify sources, labels and manufacturer procedures, restrict access, and use designated monitoring/protective equipment under training. For a novice, the correct exercise is to read the hazard information and write a safe control plan—not conduct exposure experiments.

worked.heading: Field scenario · dark optical port
worked.scenario: A rack’s fiber port appears dark. A colleague proposes peering into the connector to check for light.
steps: Reject the visual inspection: some transmission wavelengths are invisible.
Identify system status and manufacturer instructions from safe indicators.
Use only approved optical inspection/testing equipment and the organization’s laser safety procedure.
worked.conclusion: A dark port is not a demonstrated safe optical port.

check.ask: Why is looking into an apparently dark optical connector unsafe?
options: Fiber connectors cannot transmit any light.
Visible darkness always means zero optical power.
The source may emit invisible hazardous optical energy.
check.why: Optical safety cannot be judged by visible appearance alone.

source.title: ETA International: CETa Competency Requirements
source.task: Identify the separate RF exposure and optical hazards competency statements.

pages.title: Synthesis: a safe, explained, defensible decision
pages.text: The goal of this module is not to memorize warnings. It is to recognize hazards, explain their mechanisms, select an appropriate control, and document what you actually know.
pages.remember: A safe decision supported by evidence outranks a fast but uncontrolled measurement.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

paragraphs: Use the decision loop

For each situation: (1) identify all potential energy and access paths, (2) distinguish known information from assumptions, (3) choose applicable authorized controls and specialist escalation, (4) predict what a safe training observation would show, and (5) document the evidence and remaining uncertainty. If you cannot establish a safe boundary, do not proceed.
Teach back the concepts

Explain why touching a shocked person can create a second victim; why fuse current rating is only one required parameter; why a wrist strap protects electronics but does not replace isolation; why continuity must not be checked on a live circuit; and why a dark fiber connector is not proof of safety. Use the words “source,” “energy,” “path,” “verification,” and “qualification” accurately.
What a pass means

Completing this text records instruction, not physical proficiency. Your short knowledge checks are formative. The module assessment uses a stricter 100% internal safety-critical target; incorrect answers direct you back to the relevant teaching page. The course does not certify electrical work authorization, CPR competence, or compliance with a workplace safety program.

worked.heading: Capstone case · three hazards at once
worked.scenario: An unfamiliar instrument arrives with exposed power wiring, an unpackaged static-sensitive PCB and an active fiber lead. A coworker says the quickest inspection is to energize it.
steps: Recognize electrical, ESD, and optical hazards separately.
Stop the task and identify authorization, equipment procedures and approved isolation/handling methods.
Plan observations that can be made without energized exposure.
Document unresolved hazards; escalate before any physical work.
worked.conclusion: A safe decision supported by evidence outranks a fast but uncontrolled measurement.

check.ask: What is the strongest evidence-based outcome when a hazard cannot be controlled by a novice?
options: Continue carefully to finish the worksheet.
Stop and seek qualified supervision, documenting the remaining uncertainty.
Declare the equipment safe because it is for training.
check.why: Safe refusal and escalation are valid technician decisions.

source.title: NIOSH / CDC: Electrical Safety in the Workplace
source.task: Compare its qualified-person boundary with the module’s capstone decision.

examples.title: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

detail.problem: A 9 V source is connected across a 1.0 kΩ resistor. Find current and resistor power.
steps: Convert 1.0 kΩ to 1,000 Ω.
A common 0.25 W resistor has margin because 0.081 W is well below 0.25 W.
detail.answer: 9 mA and 81 mW.
detail.transfer: If the resistance were accidentally 100 Ω, current and power would each be ten times larger; that is why the value and current limit are checked before power-up.

examples.title: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

detail.problem: A 12 V source feeds a 680 ohm resistor. Predict current and resistor power, then decide whether a 1/8 W resistor is suitable.
steps: Current: I = 12 V / 680 ohm = 0.01765 A, about 17.6 mA.
A 1/8 W resistor is rated 0.125 W, below the predicted dissipation.
Choose a higher power rating and leave reasonable thermal margin rather than operating at the edge.
detail.answer: About 17.6 mA and 0.212 W; a 1/8 W resistor is not suitable.
detail.meaning: The arithmetic predicts not just a value but whether a physical component is safe to use.

examples.title: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

detail.problem: You are about to power a 5 V LED circuit. The supply shows 5.0 V and a 20 mA limit; the meter lead remains in the A jack from yesterday.
steps: Do not connect the meter across the circuit.
Move the lead to the voltage/ohms jack and select DC volts if measuring voltage.
Inspect LED polarity and series resistor; check rail-to-ground resistance with power off.
State the stop condition, then power while watching supply current.
detail.answer: Correct the meter configuration before power. A current-jack meter across the rail could short it.
detail.transfer: The same pre-power discipline is used during PCB bring-up, where current consumption is an early fault signal.

examples.title: Safe bench setup, prediction, and measurement

detail.problem: A 5 V development board is expected to draw 35-60 mA at idle. On first power with a 100 mA current limit, the supply enters CC mode at 100 mA and the output falls to 1.2 V.
steps: The low rail is not evidence of a weak 5 V supply; CC mode says the load is demanding more than the set limit.
Disable the output rather than raising the limit.
Perform power-off inspection and rail-to-ground resistance checks; compare with board documentation if available.
Look for polarity errors, solder bridges, wrong connector orientation, or a shorted peripheral before another controlled power attempt.
detail.answer: Stop and investigate the load/short path. Do not raise the current limit merely to make the rail reach 5 V.
detail.meaning: Supply mode is part of the measurement. It tells you whether voltage or current is the controlled quantity.

examples.title: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

detail.problem: A through-hole joint forms a dull ball around the lead and does not spread over the pad.
steps: This suggests inadequate wetting, contamination, insufficient heat transfer, or movement.
Inspect tip condition, surface cleanliness, flux, temperature, and whether pad and lead were heated together.
Reflow with controlled heat only if the pad is intact and the process is safe.
Inspect, continuity-check, and functionally verify afterward.
detail.answer: Treat the shape as evidence of poor wetting; correct the process, then verify electrically.
detail.transfer: The same diagnostic habit separates symptom from cause in electronics faults.

pages.title: Matter, atoms, and the origin of electric charge
pages.text: Start at the scale of matter. An atom contains a compact nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons; charge is a property of particles, not a fluid hidden inside a battery.
pages.remember: Its charge becomes negative. Total charge is conserved; electrons moved between objects.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

A proton has positive elementary charge; an electron has equal-magnitude negative charge; a neutron is neutral. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. When electrons are transferred, a body can have a net charge. In a metal, some electrons are mobile; in an insulator, charge motion is much more limited under ordinary conditions. Charging by contact or friction redistributes electrons; it does not create new total charge. Conventional current direction is defined as the direction positive charge would move, opposite to electron drift in many metal wires.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes

An atom sketch is a learning model, not a literal picture of electrons orbiting like planets. Electrical engineering usually models bulk charges, fields, and current rather than following each electron.

worked.heading: Worked study · Matter, atoms, and the origin of electric charge
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: An object loses 2 × 10¹² electrons.
Each electron has charge magnitude about 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so it becomes positively charged by about 3.204 × 10⁻⁷ C.
The sign matters: removing negative charge leaves a net positive imbalance.
worked.conclusion: Its charge becomes negative. Total charge is conserved; electrons moved between objects.

reflection.ask: If a neutral object gains electrons, what is the sign of its net charge, and what was conserved?
reflection.answer: Its charge becomes negative. Total charge is conserved; electrons moved between objects.

pages.title: What voltage measures—and why one probe is not enough
pages.text: Voltage is a difference in electric potential between two points. To state a voltage meaningfully, specify both the point being examined and its reference.
pages.remember: No. It means the red probe is 3 V below the black probe in potential at that measurement.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

A difference of one volt means one joule of energy transferred per coulomb of charge. V_AB = V_A − V_B; a negative result says point A is at lower potential than B under the chosen reference. Electrical ground is often a designated zero-volt reference, but the ground label alone does not prove a node is safe to touch. A supply might be 5 V relative to its return terminal even when no load is connected: a voltage difference is possible without ongoing current.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Do not say “this wire has five volts” without saying relative to what. Potential difference is not energy, current, or power.

worked.heading: Worked study · What voltage measures—and why one probe is not enough
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A circuit has A = 8 V and B = 3 V relative to the same reference.
V_AB = 8 − 3 = +5 V; reversing the leads gives V_BA = −5 V.
The system did not change—only the order of the comparison changed.
worked.conclusion: No. It means the red probe is 3 V below the black probe in potential at that measurement.

reflection.ask: If the meter displays −3 V across two nodes, is the voltage invalid?
reflection.answer: No. It means the red probe is 3 V below the black probe in potential at that measurement.

pages.title: Current needs a conducting path
pages.text: Current is the rate of charge crossing a chosen boundary: I = ΔQ/Δt. Charge can be present even when no continuous current flows.
pages.remember: A closed conducting path from the source through the resistor and back to the source, with potential difference to drive current.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

One ampere is one coulomb per second. In an ordinary steady DC circuit, the supply, conductor, load and return form a closed path. Opening a series connection ideally reduces steady current through that branch to zero, while the source can still maintain its terminal voltage. Real capacitors briefly carry charging currents, and real leakage paths complicate an ideal open-circuit model; those effects come later. Current is not consumed by a resistor: electrical energy is transferred while charge is conserved.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Never connect a meter in its current range straight across a source to “see how much current it has.” That makes a low-resistance path through the meter and can be dangerous.

worked.heading: Worked study · Current needs a conducting path
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: If 0.18 C of charge passes through a point during 0.030 s, the average current is 0.18/0.030 = 6 A.
If the switch is open and only 5 V appears across the terminals, the ideal steady current is zero despite the voltage.
worked.conclusion: A closed conducting path from the source through the resistor and back to the source, with potential difference to drive current.

reflection.ask: What must be present for steady current in a simple battery-and-resistor circuit?
reflection.answer: A closed conducting path from the source through the resistor and back to the source, with potential difference to drive current.

pages.title: SI prefixes: communicating scale without losing units
pages.text: Electronics deals with extremely different scales: microamperes, milliamperes, kilohms and megohms all appear on a single workbench.
pages.remember: 47 mA. One ampere is 1000 milliamperes, so multiply the ampere value by 1000.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

The prefix is a power-of-ten multiplier. k = 10³, M = 10⁶, m = 10⁻³, µ = 10⁻⁶, n = 10⁻⁹, p = 10⁻¹². Uppercase M (mega) and lowercase m (milli) differ by a factor of one billion. In scientific notation, move the decimal until the coefficient is between 1 and 10 and count places. In engineering notation, use exponents divisible by three. Always carry units through each calculation; adding ohms to volts or comparing 5 mA with 5 A without conversion is an error.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes

NIST SI style uses symbols without plurals (not “5 kΩs”), a space between number and unit (5 V), and case-sensitive prefixes. Symbol style is not a cosmetic preference when the wrong case changes a component value.

worked.conclusion: 47 mA. One ampere is 1000 milliamperes, so multiply the ampere value by 1000.

reflection.ask: Convert 0.047 A into milliamperes and explain the factor.
reflection.answer: 47 mA. One ampere is 1000 milliamperes, so multiply the ampere value by 1000.

pages.title: Resistance as a measured relationship, not a mysterious force
pages.text: Resistance tells us how much voltage across an ohmic device is required to sustain a given current through it.
pages.remember: Current becomes half as large, because I = V/R.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

For an ohmic resistor at approximately fixed temperature, V = IR. The slope of a voltage-versus-current graph is R when voltage is on the vertical axis. The ratio need not stay constant for diodes, lamps that heat up, and many semiconductor devices. Electrical resistance depends on material, geometry and temperature; this course starts with the ideal constant-resistance model and makes its limits explicit.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Ohm’s law is not a license to apply V = IR to an unknown nonlinear component at any operating point. Identify the element and the conditions first.

worked.heading: Worked study · Resistance as a measured relationship, not a mysterious force
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 470 Ω resistor connected across an ideal 9 V source has I = 9/470 A ≈ 0.0191 A = 19.1 mA.
Double the resistance while keeping 9 V: expected current halves to about 9.57 mA.
This is a model prediction, not a reason to connect unverified hardware.
worked.conclusion: Current becomes half as large, because I = V/R.

reflection.ask: If voltage stays fixed and a resistor value doubles, what happens to current in the ideal model?
reflection.answer: Current becomes half as large, because I = V/R.

pages.title: Sources, DC, AC, and the meaning of a waveform
pages.text: A source supplies electrical energy or establishes a controlled voltage or current. Different source models predict different circuit behavior.
pages.remember: Yes. With the circuit open, the supply can maintain a voltage difference while ideal steady external current is zero.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

A battery is a chemical energy source; a solar cell converts light; a generator converts mechanical energy; an electronic supply converts and regulates power. DC describes a quantity whose polarity does not reverse (it may still vary in magnitude). AC changes direction or polarity with time, commonly in periodic cycles. Later you will study peak, RMS, frequency and phase carefully; here the point is to identify the correct source and reference before using a formula. Real sources have limits, including internal resistance and current capacity.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Do not confuse the maximum current printed on a supply with current that is always forced into every load. The load and regulation determine current within the supply’s limits.

worked.heading: Worked study · Sources, DC, AC, and the meaning of a waveform
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A regulated 5 V USB source feeding a 100 Ω resistor would ideally provide 50 mA and dissipate 0.25 W in the resistor.
An unloaded 5 V label does not guarantee the supply will still deliver 5 V if asked for more current than it is rated to provide.
worked.conclusion: Yes. With the circuit open, the supply can maintain a voltage difference while ideal steady external current is zero.

reflection.ask: Can a 5 V DC supply have 5 V at its terminals but 0 A through the external circuit?
reflection.answer: Yes. With the circuit open, the supply can maintain a voltage difference while ideal steady external current is zero.

pages.title: Electrical power: when movement of charge becomes heat
pages.text: Power measures the rate of energy transfer. In a circuit, voltage and current together determine the rate of electrical work.
pages.remember: P = V²/R, so at fixed R doubling voltage quadruples power.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

P = VI, with watts equal to volts times amperes. For an ohmic resistor, substituting V = IR gives P = I²R and P = V²/R. These are related ways of describing the same dissipated power. Energy is P × time, so a 1 W load operating for 10 seconds converts 10 joules. Real resistors turn most electrical energy into heat; a component rating is a limit under specified mounting and ambient conditions, not a guarantee of cool operation.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
A correct current calculation is not enough to establish component suitability. Always calculate power and check the device data.

worked.heading: Worked study · Electrical power: when movement of charge becomes heat
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 1 kΩ resistor on 12 V carries 12 mA and dissipates 0.144 W.
A nominal 0.125 W resistor is undersized for this ideal condition, even if the measured voltage seems ordinary.
A 0.25 W part provides a numerical margin, subject to thermal conditions and derating.
worked.conclusion: P = V²/R, so at fixed R doubling voltage quadruples power.

reflection.ask: Why can the same resistor overheat when applied voltage doubles?
reflection.answer: P = V²/R, so at fixed R doubling voltage quadruples power.

pages.title: Graphs, slopes, and the first look at decibels
pages.text: Graphs reveal relationships that a single number cannot show: they display which quantity is changing and what stays fixed.
pages.remember: Resistance: ΔV/ΔI in ohms, under conditions where that ratio is stable.
pages.sourceLesson: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

Read an axis label before interpreting a slope. For an I-versus-V plot, slope is ΔI/ΔV (conductance, 1/R) when current is vertical; for a V-versus-I plot, slope is resistance. A straight line through the origin suggests ohmic behavior under the measured conditions. Decibels compare ratios logarithmically: for power, 10 log10(P2/P1) dB; for voltage across equal impedances, 20 log10(V2/V1) dB. We introduce those separately because using the voltage formula on unequal impedances can mislead.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
A graph without axis units or a reference condition is not trustworthy technician evidence. “Gain = 6 dB” needs the ratio type and context.

worked.heading: Worked study · Graphs, slopes, and the first look at decibels
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A test record shows 0.5 V, 1.0 V and 1.5 V across a resistor for 1, 2 and 3 mA respectively.
From ΔV/ΔI = 0.5 V/0.001 A, R = 500 Ω.
A doubling of power corresponds to about +3.01 dB; halving gives −3.01 dB.
worked.conclusion: Resistance: ΔV/ΔI in ohms, under conditions where that ratio is stable.

reflection.ask: For a voltage-vertical/current-horizontal graph, what does slope represent?
reflection.answer: Resistance: ΔV/ΔI in ohms, under conditions where that ratio is stable.

pages.title: Energy, component ratings, and numerical reasonableness
pages.text: Before you trust a calculated number, ask whether its scale and units make physical sense.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

Energy is accumulated power. A watt is one joule per second. Components have voltage, current, power, temperature and sometimes pulse/energy ratings; these are different constraints. A result of 25 A in a breadboard LED branch should trigger a units and circuit check rather than uncritical acceptance. Dimensional analysis catches many mistakes: V/Ω gives amperes, A × V gives watts, W × s gives joules. A realistic measurement report records the predicted value, actual value, conditions and uncertainty sources.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Never let a plausible-looking calculator display override an engineering sanity check. Check orders of magnitude before touching equipment.

worked.heading: Worked study · Energy, component ratings, and numerical reasonableness
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 5 V resistor circuit calculated to draw 2 mA should dissipate 10 mW.
If a spreadsheet outputs “10 W,” inspect whether 2 mA was entered as 2 A.
One missing milli-prefix causes a thousandfold power error.

reflection.ask: Why is 2 mA × 5 V equal to 10 mW rather than 10 W?

examples.title: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

detail.problem: A 9 V source is connected across a 1.0 kΩ resistor. Find current and resistor power.
steps: Convert 1.0 kΩ to 1,000 Ω.
A common 0.25 W resistor has margin because 0.081 W is well below 0.25 W.
detail.answer: 9 mA and 81 mW.
detail.transfer: If the resistance were accidentally 100 Ω, current and power would each be ten times larger; that is why the value and current limit are checked before power-up.

examples.title: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

detail.problem: A 12 V source feeds a 680 ohm resistor. Predict current and resistor power, then decide whether a 1/8 W resistor is suitable.
steps: Current: I = 12 V / 680 ohm = 0.01765 A, about 17.6 mA.
A 1/8 W resistor is rated 0.125 W, below the predicted dissipation.
Choose a higher power rating and leave reasonable thermal margin rather than operating at the edge.
detail.answer: About 17.6 mA and 0.212 W; a 1/8 W resistor is not suitable.
detail.meaning: The arithmetic predicts not just a value but whether a physical component is safe to use.

examples.title: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

detail.problem: A 12 V source feeds 2 kΩ in series with 4 kΩ. Find current, both drops, and unloaded output across 4 kΩ.
steps: RT = 2 kΩ + 4 kΩ = 6 kΩ.
I = 12 V / 6 kΩ = 2 mA.
V2k = 2 mA × 2 kΩ = 4 V.
V4k = 2 mA × 4 kΩ = 8 V.
KVL check: 4 V + 8 V = 12 V.
detail.answer: 2 mA, 4 V, and 8 V.
detail.transfer: If a 4 kΩ load is attached across the lower 4 kΩ, the lower equivalent becomes 2 kΩ; the output becomes 6 V, not 8 V.

examples.title: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

detail.problem: A 12 V divider uses 3.3 kOhm on top and 2.2 kOhm on bottom. Find unloaded Vout, then find Vout when a 2.2 kOhm load is connected from output to ground.
steps: Loaded lower leg: 2.2 kOhm || 2.2 kOhm = 1.1 kOhm.
The heavy load changes the circuit substantially; the original divider equation using 2.2 kOhm alone is no longer valid.
detail.answer: 4.8 V unloaded and 3.0 V with the 2.2 kOhm load.
detail.meaning: A connected instrument or downstream stage can become part of the network and change the value being measured.

examples.title: Waveform language and energy-storage behavior

detail.problem: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 10 µF capacitor from a 5 V step. Find τ and approximate voltage after one τ.
steps: After one τ, the capacitor has completed about 63% of the change.
After about 5τ = 0.5 s, it is near the final value.
detail.answer: τ = 0.1 s; Vc at one τ is about 3.15 V.
detail.transfer: A scope cursor can test both the predicted time and voltage on the charging curve.

guided.text: A 3.3 V source is applied to 1.5 kOhm. Calculate current, then state whether 1 mA or 10 mA is the more sensible mental estimate before calculating.
A resistor carries 20 mA with 5 V across it. Find resistance and power. Keep units through every step.
Sketch a source, resistor, return path, and reference node. Mark where a voltmeter connects and where an ammeter would have to be inserted.
Draw a node-labeled circuit with a 10 V source and two 1 kOhm series resistors. Predict the midpoint voltage and verify KVL around the loop.
At a node, 5 mA enters while 1.5 mA and 2 mA leave through two branches. Use KCL to find the third branch current and state its direction.
A 5 V divider uses 10 kOhm over 10 kOhm. Recalculate the output if a 10 kOhm meter input is connected to the midpoint.

teachBack: Explain voltage, current, resistance, and power to a new technician without using a formula triangle. Then use one resistor example to show how the four quantities connect and why a power rating matters.
Explain series, parallel, KCL, KVL, and loading without relying on memorized formulas. Use one labeled-node circuit and show how conservation predicts what a meter should read.

Explain why capacitor voltage and inductor current cannot change instantaneously in the ideal model. Use one RC time-constant example and one inductive flyback example to connect the equations to observed waveforms.

questions.prompt: What is 4.7 kΩ expressed in ohms?

questions.prompt: What is 3 × 10⁻³ amperes in milliamperes?

questions.prompt: A voltage-versus-time graph rises 2 V in 4 ms. What is its average slope?

A meter cannot show negative voltage
The current flows backward at exactly 3 A

choices: The volt is a unit of time
Power cannot be computed from voltage and current

pages.title: Resistor families and why construction matters
pages.text: A resistor is not merely a number of ohms. Its construction affects stability, noise, power, pulse handling and behavior at higher frequencies.
pages.remember: The wound conductor adds parasitic inductance, changing impedance at higher frequencies.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

Common fixed resistors include carbon composition, carbon film, metal film, metal oxide and wirewound types. Metal film parts often offer good tolerance and temperature stability. Wirewound elements can handle substantial power but their winding may add inductance. Surface-mount chip resistors trade different package and thermal constraints. Specialized resistive devices include thermistors, photoresistors and potentiometers; their values change deliberately with temperature, light or mechanical adjustment.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
A resistor symbol describes circuit function but cannot tell you its package, temperature coefficient, tolerance or allowable dissipated power.

worked.heading: Worked study · Resistor families and why construction matters
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 100 Ω 0.25 W chip and a 100 Ω 5 W wirewound part share nominal resistance but are not interchangeable in a high-power, high-frequency circuit.
Compare mechanical, electrical and environmental requirements rather than matching the printed ohms alone.
worked.conclusion: The wound conductor adds parasitic inductance, changing impedance at higher frequencies.

reflection.ask: Why might a wirewound resistor behave poorly in a fast RF circuit even if its DC ohms are correct?
reflection.answer: The wound conductor adds parasitic inductance, changing impedance at higher frequencies.

pages.title: Selecting a resistor: four separate checks
pages.text: A replacement resistor must meet the electrical and physical demands of the circuit, not just the nominal resistance.
pages.remember: Yes. The permitted range is 423–517 Ω.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

Check resistance value, tolerance, continuous power rating, and applicable voltage/pulse/environmental limits. Tolerance ±5% on 1 kΩ allows 950–1050 Ω before considering temperature effects. Power rating assumes conditions described by the manufacturer; mounting, airflow and ambient temperature affect achievable dissipation. A temperature coefficient in ppm/°C predicts incremental drift. If a part is burned, first determine why it overheated rather than immediately fitting a larger resistor.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Do not measure resistance on a powered board. Other connected components can affect an in-circuit resistance reading, so a low reading alone does not prove a defective resistor.

worked.heading: Worked study · Selecting a resistor: four separate checks
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 2.2 kΩ ±5% resistor may range from 2.09 to 2.31 kΩ.
A measured 2.16 kΩ is within tolerance.
A measured 1.1 kΩ might indicate the wrong part or in-circuit parallel paths; isolate a lead only when safe and authorized before concluding.
worked.conclusion: Yes. The permitted range is 423–517 Ω.

reflection.ask: A 470 Ω ±10% resistor reads 505 Ω in suitable isolated measurement. Is it within tolerance?
reflection.answer: Yes. The permitted range is 423–517 Ω.

pages.title: Deriving Ohm’s law rather than memorizing triangles
pages.text: In the ideal linear-resistor model, the current is proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

The relationship V = IR becomes I = V/R if current is unknown and R = V/I if resistance is unknown. Rearranging is ordinary algebra: divide both sides by the quantity you are removing. Keep units attached. Amperes × ohms = volts; volts ÷ ohms = amperes. A circuit diagram and a consistent choice of reference directions are prerequisites for using the equation correctly.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Do not choose the formula first and the circuit second. Identify voltage across the named resistor and current through that same resistor.

worked.heading: Worked study · Deriving Ohm’s law rather than memorizing triangles
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 6.0 V source drives 20 mA through an ideal resistor.
The backward check is 0.020 A × 300 Ω = 6.0 V.
If the result had been 0.3 Ω, the prefix was probably lost.

reflection.ask: What resistance carries 15 mA when it has 3.3 V across it?

pages.title: When Ohm’s-law predictions can fail
pages.text: A constant resistance is a model. The model is powerful precisely because we know when to stop trusting it.
pages.remember: No. The LED has a nonlinear current–voltage characteristic; use its datasheet and a current-limiting design.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

A metal-film resistor near room temperature often behaves approximately ohmically. A hot filament changes resistance with temperature; LEDs and diodes are nonlinear, and semiconductors have operating regions. Real sources have internal resistance and finite current capability. A technician predicts with a justified model, measures under known conditions, then reconciles disagreement without automatically calling the meter wrong.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
A single V/I measurement does not demonstrate linearity over the full operating range; several operating points are needed.

worked.heading: Worked study · When Ohm’s-law predictions can fail
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A nominal 1 kΩ part should draw 5 mA at 5 V.
If measurement shows 4.6 mA, plausible causes include resistor tolerance, source droop, meter burden, lead configuration or an incorrect test point.
Record the actual measured voltage across the resistor and compute V/I before guessing.
worked.conclusion: No. The LED has a nonlinear current–voltage characteristic; use its datasheet and a current-limiting design.

reflection.ask: An LED draws 10 mA at one forward voltage. Can you infer it will draw exactly 20 mA at twice that voltage?
reflection.answer: No. The LED has a nonlinear current–voltage characteristic; use its datasheet and a current-limiting design.

pages.title: Source, resistor and load form a power budget
pages.text: Once voltage and current are known, the resistor’s heating and the source’s burden can be quantified.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

For an ohmic resistor P = VI = I²R = V²/R. These formulas yield the same result when values refer to the same component and operating point. A source’s rating describes its operating envelope and does not imply each load is forced to take the maximum. In a series LED circuit, the LED has a forward voltage drop and the resistor sees the remaining supply voltage; do not calculate resistor power from the entire source voltage.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
A resistor calculated to run exactly at its nominal power rating has no design margin. Use appropriate derating and manufacturer specifications.

worked.heading: Worked study · Source, resistor and load form a power budget
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 9 V battery supplies an LED with 2 V forward drop through 470 Ω.
Ideal resistor drop is 7 V; current ≈ 14.9 mA; resistor P = 7 × 0.0149 ≈ 0.104 W.
That is less than 0.25 W at room temperature, but thermal and component specifications still matter.

reflection.ask: With 12 V across a 1 kΩ resistor, what power is dissipated?

pages.title: Power ratings explain heat, not just math
pages.text: The watts printed on a resistor specification reflect its ability to dissipate heat within stated operating conditions.
pages.remember: The stated rating depends on ambient temperature, mounting and derating; the real operating conditions may reduce permissible power.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

Electrical power converted in the resistor produces heat. The component’s temperature rise depends on thermal path, PCB copper area, lead length, enclosure ventilation and surrounding temperature. A resistor rated 0.25 W at a reference ambient may need substantial derating in a hot cabinet. High pulse energy can damage a device even when average power appears low; apply the relevant pulse/overload rating.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Touch is not an approved temperature measurement method, and a resistor that appears physically intact may have drifted after overheating.

worked.heading: Worked study · Power ratings explain heat, not just math
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: At 24 V across 2.2 kΩ, P ≈ 0.262 W.
This is already greater than 0.25 W, even before considering ambient derating.
The right fix may be a higher-rated resistor with correct dimensions or a circuit redesign, not an improvised parallel connection.
worked.conclusion: The stated rating depends on ambient temperature, mounting and derating; the real operating conditions may reduce permissible power.

reflection.ask: Why can a 0.5 W resistor be unsuitable for 0.4 W continuous dissipation?
reflection.answer: The stated rating depends on ambient temperature, mounting and derating; the real operating conditions may reduce permissible power.

pages.title: Comparing P = VI, I²R and V²/R
pages.text: Choose the power relationship using the quantities you know, not whichever form is easiest to memorize.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

If V and I are measured at a component, P = VI. If I and R are known for an ohmic resistor, P = I²R. If V and R are known, P = V²/R. These are algebraically linked by Ohm’s law, but the alternate forms cannot be blindly applied to non-ohmic devices. The resistor power rating is a separate engineering constraint, not an additional factor in the equation.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Before accepting an answer, compare it to a second formula. If two forms disagree, your current, voltage or resistance inputs are inconsistent.

worked.heading: Worked study · Comparing P = VI, I²R and V²/R
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 330 Ω resistor carries 30 mA.
Using V = IR gives 9.9 V, and P = 9.9 × 0.030 = 0.297 W.
A 0.25 W part is unsuitable under that continuous condition.

reflection.ask: A 200 Ω resistor dissipates 0.5 W. What approximate RMS or DC current flows under the ohmic model?

pages.title: Failure clues from resistor type and environment
pages.text: Good troubleshooting connects observed behavior to the part’s construction and how it was used.
pages.remember: It is the adjustable contact that divides the resistive track and allows a selectable output voltage or resistance.
pages.sourceLesson: Component families, ratings, magnetism, and machines

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

A wirewound resistor may be physically intact yet fail at high frequencies because of inductance; a thermistor may read quite differently cold and hot; a pot may have an intermittent wiper contact. Overheated resistors can rise or fall in resistance or fail open, depending on type and damage. Soot or discoloration is a clue, not a definitive electrical diagnosis. Compare with the schematic, expected operating conditions and device datasheet.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Do not infer the original circuit fault from a scorched component without checking why that part dissipated excessive power.

worked.heading: Worked study · Failure clues from resistor type and environment
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: An NTC thermistor measures 10 kΩ at a specified reference temperature.
Warm it gently within allowed limits and the resistance normally decreases.
A fixed 10 kΩ metal-film resistor should not show such a dramatic temperature-dependent change under similar benign conditions.
worked.conclusion: It is the adjustable contact that divides the resistive track and allows a selectable output voltage or resistance.

reflection.ask: What is the purpose of the wiper in a potentiometer?
reflection.answer: It is the adjustable contact that divides the resistive track and allows a selectable output voltage or resistance.

pages.title: Measuring resistance without being fooled by the circuit
pages.text: An ohmmeter applies its own small test stimulus. It is intended for de-energized circuits under the instrument’s specifications.
pages.remember: A second 1 kΩ path in parallel makes the equivalent resistance 500 Ω.
pages.sourceLesson: The four quantities and the circuit they describe

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

A resistance measurement with other components still connected often sees more than the target resistor. Parallel current paths lower the apparent resistance; semiconductor junctions can make readings depend on polarity and range. Plan a safe isolation step before disconnection and never probe an energized circuit in resistance or continuity mode. When precision matters, account for lead resistance and range specification.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
A continuity beep only means the meter detects a low-resistance path under its threshold; it does not certify current capacity or safe wiring.

worked.heading: Worked study · Measuring resistance without being fooled by the circuit
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: Two 1 kΩ resistors in parallel look like 500 Ω to an ohmmeter across the pair.
Concluding that either individual resistor is 500 Ω would be a topology error.
A measured 499 Ω is plausible for the pair even though each part remains about 1 kΩ.
worked.conclusion: A second 1 kΩ path in parallel makes the equivalent resistance 500 Ω.

reflection.ask: Why can an in-circuit 1 kΩ resistor read about 500 Ω?
reflection.answer: A second 1 kΩ path in parallel makes the equivalent resistance 500 Ω.

pages.title: Potentiometers and loaded voltage dividers
pages.text: A potentiometer uses a movable contact to divide one resistor into two parts; as a divider it converts a source voltage into a selected fraction.
pages.remember: The load lowers the effective bottom resistance, shifting the division ratio while increasing source current.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

For an unloaded divider, Vout = Vin × Rbottom/(Rtop + Rbottom) measured relative to the bottom node. The slider position changes the ratio. When an external load attaches to the wiper, its resistance lies in parallel with the lower segment and draws additional current; Vout generally moves away from the ideal unloaded value. This is why voltage dividers are useful as references/signal settings but not automatically good power supplies.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
A pot whose wiper loses contact can cause uncontrolled output behavior; safety-critical controls require appropriate fail-safe design.

worked.heading: Worked study · Potentiometers and loaded voltage dividers
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: A 10 kΩ pot on 5 V with the wiper halfway yields about 2.5 V unloaded.
Attach a 5 kΩ load from wiper to return: the lower 5 kΩ section is in parallel with 5 kΩ, yielding 2.5 kΩ.
worked.conclusion: The load lowers the effective bottom resistance, shifting the division ratio while increasing source current.

reflection.ask: Why does a heavy load reduce the output of a simple resistive divider?
reflection.answer: The load lowers the effective bottom resistance, shifting the division ratio while increasing source current.

pages.title: Reading resistor markings and tolerance bands
pages.text: Identifying a resistor is a combined visual, mathematical and documentation task. Begin with package type and the manufacturer convention.
pages.remember: 10 × 10³ Ω = 10 kΩ with ±5% tolerance.
pages.sourceLesson: Series, parallel, KVL, KCL, and divider reasoning

paragraphs: Build the underlying model

On a typical four-band axial resistor, the first two bands are significant digits, the third is a power-of-ten multiplier and the fourth is tolerance. Brown = 1, black = 0, red multiplier = 10², so brown–black–red represents 1000 Ω. Gold tolerance is ±5%. Surface-mount parts often use three- or four-character codes, and some very small parts have no printed value. Confirm unfamiliar markings against a trusted chart and measure a disconnected part when safe.
Interpretation, limits and common mistakes
Color-banding is not a substitute for part numbers, thermal ratings or tolerance verification on an unknown device.

worked.heading: Worked study · Reading resistor markings and tolerance bands
worked.scenario: Follow the worked case in sequence. Pause after each statement to predict the next step.
steps: Yellow–violet–red–gold indicates 47 × 100 = 4700 Ω, ±5%, nominal 4.7 kΩ.
The permissible range is 4465–4935 Ω.
The gold band normally marks the tolerance end; do not assume all resistor marking systems have identical band placement.
worked.conclusion: 10 × 10³ Ω = 10 kΩ with ±5% tolerance.

reflection.ask: What nominal value is brown–black–orange–gold in the standard four-band convention?
reflection.answer: 10 × 10³ Ω = 10 kΩ with ±5% tolerance.
