pages.title: Darlington, IGBT and CMOS context
pages.text: A Darlington pair offers high current gain but generally has greater VBE and VCE(sat) costs than a single BJT.
pages.remember: Its saturation drop can be larger, producing greater V×I dissipation.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A Darlington pair offers high current gain but generally has greater VBE and VCE(sat) costs than a single BJT. An IGBT combines MOS-gate input behavior with bipolar conduction suited to some higher-voltage systems. CMOS integrates complementary MOS devices, often with low static power but significant transition currents.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Complex devices cannot be swapped solely because both are 'transistors.' This module does not train unsupervised high-energy IGBT service.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Darlington, IGBT and CMOS context
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Choose device family by switching frequency, voltage, drive, loss, and safe operating limits: a tiny battery CMOS logic gate is not a power IGBT, while a Darlington can be convenient for a modest relay with a known drop budget.
worked.conclusion: Its saturation drop can be larger, producing greater V×I dissipation.

reflection.ask: Why might a Darlington run hotter than a suitable MOSFET at the same load?
reflection.answer: Its saturation drop can be larger, producing greater V×I dissipation.

pages.title: Transistor competency integration case
pages.text: Combine bias, load, gate/base requirements, heat and expected measurements into one reasoning chain.
pages.remember: Verified voltages/currents under both states, correct protection, part ratings and documented repeatable setup.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Combine bias, load, gate/base requirements, heat and expected measurements into one reasoning chain. State what information a datasheet must supply before a technician declares a replacement suitable. Identify whether the transistor is used as a switch, amplifier, current source or protection element.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
The exercise is a paper or simulation case unless actual safely captured measurements and setup records are provided.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Transistor competency integration case
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A 12 V, 0.3 A relay is controlled with a low-side transistor.
Record input logic voltage, load current, coil inductance, clamping diode, transistor on-state loss, safe drive, and expected DMM/scope observations for both on/off states.
worked.conclusion: Verified voltages/currents under both states, correct protection, part ratings and documented repeatable setup.

reflection.ask: What constitutes stronger evidence than merely observing the relay click?
reflection.answer: Verified voltages/currents under both states, correct protection, part ratings and documented repeatable setup.

examples.title: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

detail.problem: A 5 V supply drives a red LED approximated at 1.9 V with a 330 Ω resistor. Estimate current and resistor power.
steps: Resistor voltage = 5 − 1.9 = 3.1 V.
P resistor = I²R ≈ 0.029 W.
Verify the actual LED datasheet and current target; forward voltage is not exact.
detail.answer: About 9.4 mA and 29 mW in the resistor.
detail.transfer: This same load current becomes the minimum current the transistor switch must handle.

examples.title: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

detail.problem: A low-side N-channel MOSFET switches a 12 V, 0.5 A load. The MOSFET has Rds(on)=0.08 ohm at the stated gate drive. Estimate conduction loss.
steps: This low conduction loss is only valid at the gate voltage for which Rds(on) is specified.
Switching losses, thermal environment, transients, and load type still require checking.
If the datasheet specifies Rds(on) only at 10 V gate drive, a 3.3 V MCU may not turn the device on fully.
detail.answer: About 20 mW conduction loss under the stated Rds(on) condition.
detail.meaning: A transistor part number is not enough; the control voltage and datasheet test condition determine the actual switching behavior.

examples.title: Design and diagnose a protected low-side switch

detail.problem: An N-MOSFET low-side switch leaves the motor off. Gate is 3.3 V relative to source, drain remains 12 V, and the motor has continuity.
steps: The command reaches the gate and the load path is not obviously open.
Drain staying high means the MOSFET is not pulling down.
Check exact pinout/orientation and whether RDS(on) is specified at 3.3 V.
Power off before continuity/diode checks; replace only after configuration and rating evidence.
detail.answer: Focus on MOSFET orientation, gate-drive suitability, or device damage.
detail.transfer: The measurements isolate the switch stage without blaming firmware or motor first.

examples.title: Design and diagnose a protected low-side switch

detail.problem: A 3.3 V GPIO drives an N-MOSFET gate. The load is 200 mA at 12 V. GPIO reads HIGH in software, but the drain remains at 12 V and the load is off.
steps: Measure gate-to-source voltage, not gate-to-board-label alone.
If Vgs is near 0 V, investigate GPIO pin mux, wiring, common ground/source reference, or pull-down shorting the signal.
If Vgs is 3.3 V but drain stays 12 V, check whether the MOSFET is specified for low Rds(on) at 3.3 V, verify pinout/orientation, source connection, and device health.
If drain goes low but load is still off, move to load/supply continuity and current measurement.
detail.answer: Use gate-to-source, drain, and load-current evidence to identify which layer is failing before replacing the MOSFET.
detail.meaning: Software state and physical switch behavior are separate facts that must be connected by measurement.

examples.title: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

detail.problem: An inverting op-amp uses Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 47 kΩ, and Vin = 0.20 V. Find ideal output.
steps: Check whether the supply rails and input common-mode permit this result.
Check load and bandwidth before expecting the ideal value physically.
detail.answer: Ideal Vout = −0.94 V.
detail.transfer: If powered from a single 0–5 V supply with no bias, a negative output request will clip near the lower rail.

pages.title: Power-supply blocks from source to load
pages.text: A supply converts energy from one form or voltage level to a controlled electrical output.
pages.remember: It controls output polarity but not ripple or regulation under changing line/load conditions.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A supply converts energy from one form or voltage level to a controlled electrical output. Model it as source → protection/isolation → transformation/conversion → rectification when needed → filtering → regulation → load. The order depends on topology; modern switch-mode designs often rectify before a high-frequency transformer.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
A block diagram is a functional model, not proof every commercial supply has identical internals. Never open line-powered supplies for a course exercise.

steps: Trace an isolated low-voltage AC training source through a bridge and storage capacitor to a regulator.

worked.conclusion: It controls output polarity but not ripple or regulation under changing line/load conditions.

reflection.ask: Why doesn't a bridge rectifier alone create a steady 5 V output?
reflection.answer: It controls output polarity but not ripple or regulation under changing line/load conditions.

pages.title: Rectification and peak-voltage reasoning
pages.text: Sinewave RMS voltage is not the same as its peak.
pages.remember: RMS is a heating-equivalent measure; sinusoidal peak is √2 times RMS.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Sinewave RMS voltage is not the same as its peak. For a sine wave, Vpeak≈Vrms×√2. A bridge diode pair drops some voltage while conducting; average DC meter readings depend on meter method, waveform shape and filtering.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Transformers sag under load and diode voltage depends on current. Do not use unsafe mains measurements to check a textbook arithmetic example.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Rectification and peak-voltage reasoning
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: For isolated 9 Vrms sine, peak≈12.73 V.
Assume roughly 0.7 V per conducting silicon diode at load: bridge peak after two junctions≈11.3 V before ripple.
This is a first approximation, not a promised loaded output.
worked.conclusion: RMS is a heating-equivalent measure; sinusoidal peak is √2 times RMS.

reflection.ask: Why is 9 Vrms not equivalent to 9 Vpeak?
reflection.answer: RMS is a heating-equivalent measure; sinusoidal peak is √2 times RMS.

pages.title: Half-wave and full-wave ripple frequency
pages.text: The time between replenishment peaks determines how far a smoothing capacitor droops.
pages.remember: It replenishes the capacitor twice as frequently, reducing discharge interval.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

The time between replenishment peaks determines how far a smoothing capacitor droops. Half-wave rectification refills once per source cycle; full-wave refills twice per cycle. A 60 Hz input yields nominal 60 Hz or 120 Hz ripple respectively before considering regulation.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
This is a first-order approximate ripple estimate; high ripple violates the small-ripple approximation and ESR/load changes the waveform.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Half-wave and full-wave ripple frequency
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Compare 60 Hz half-wave and full-wave designs with identical C=1000 µF and Iload=0.1 A.
Estimate ripple ΔV≈I/(fripple C): 1.67 V for half-wave versus 0.83 V for full-wave, under simplified assumptions.
worked.conclusion: It replenishes the capacitor twice as frequently, reducing discharge interval.

reflection.ask: Why does a full-wave bridge usually yield less ripple than half-wave with the same filter?
reflection.answer: It replenishes the capacitor twice as frequently, reducing discharge interval.

pages.title: Reservoir capacitors and safe polarity
pages.text: A reservoir capacitor holds charge near peaks and supplies load current between peaks.
pages.remember: A given removed charge produces less ΔV because ΔV=ΔQ/C.
pages.sourceLesson: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A reservoir capacitor holds charge near peaks and supplies load current between peaks. Electrolytic capacitors often have polarity and voltage limits, ESR, ripple-current heating and aging behavior. Size for maximum peak input, transient margins and temperature rather than only nominal DC output.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Stored charge persists after supply removal; a discharged label or unplugged cable proves nothing. Never touch energized or charged mains-supply internals.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Reservoir capacitors and safe polarity
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: For 100 mA, 120 Hz ripple and desired roughly 1 V peak-to-peak, C≈0.1/(120×1)=833 µF; choose an appropriate standard capacitor with sufficient voltage and ripple-current ratings.
worked.conclusion: A given removed charge produces less ΔV because ΔV=ΔQ/C.

reflection.ask: Why does larger capacitance generally reduce supply ripple at a fixed load?
reflection.answer: A given removed charge produces less ΔV because ΔV=ΔQ/C.

pages.title: Linear regulators and headroom
pages.text: Linear regulators vary internal series conduction to hold output close to target.
pages.remember: The regulator loses control and output follows input or sags below its setpoint.
pages.sourceLesson: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Linear regulators vary internal series conduction to hold output close to target. They require a specified input-output headroom (dropout) and dissipate the difference between input and output as heat. Current limiting and thermal shutdown are protective functions, not permission to design without heat analysis.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
A regulator cannot maintain 5 V if the input sags below output plus required dropout. Not all three-pin devices share pinout.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Linear regulators and headroom
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A 12 V input, 5 V output at 0.2 A means regulator loss≈(12−5)×0.2=1.4 W (ignoring quiescent current).
Check device/package thermal data before assuming continuous operation.
worked.conclusion: The regulator loses control and output follows input or sags below its setpoint.

reflection.ask: What happens if the reservoir voltage dips below dropout headroom?
reflection.answer: The regulator loses control and output follows input or sags below its setpoint.

pages.title: Adjustable regulator feedback examples
pages.text: Some adjustable linear regulators use a reference voltage and external resistor divider to establish output.
pages.remember: The regulator uses the divider to compare output against its internal reference and adjusts the pass element.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Some adjustable linear regulators use a reference voltage and external resistor divider to establish output. The required circuit and resistor tolerances must come from the manufacturer's datasheet; adjustment pin current can create an error.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Do not connect a resistor network by memory to an unknown regulator. Verify pins, bypass recommendations and safe headroom.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Adjustable regulator feedback examples
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: For an LM317-style regulator, ideal approximation Vout≈1.25×(1+R2/R1).
With R1=240 Ω and R2=720 Ω, Vout≈5.0 V before adjustment-current correction; check actual device and thermal limits.
worked.conclusion: The regulator uses the divider to compare output against its internal reference and adjusts the pass element.

reflection.ask: Why does replacing a resistor in the feedback divider change output voltage?
reflection.answer: The regulator uses the divider to compare output against its internal reference and adjusts the pass element.

pages.title: Power supplies under changing loads
pages.text: Line regulation describes response to changing input; load regulation describes response to changing output current.
pages.remember: Ripple, transients, current limit or noise may still violate operating requirements.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Line regulation describes response to changing input; load regulation describes response to changing output current. A regulator can show good DC numbers and still have poor startup, transient or high-frequency behavior. The technician needs an expected window, not only an exact nominal figure.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
A DMM average value can hide short transient dips; a scope reveals startup overshoot and ripple if probed safely.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Power supplies under changing loads
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A 5.00 V no-load output falls to 4.88 V at a specified load.
Voltage change is 0.12 V, or 2.4% of 5 V reference.
Check whether that meets the product's operating limits before declaring a failure.
worked.conclusion: Ripple, transients, current limit or noise may still violate operating requirements.

reflection.ask: Why isn't '5 V on the DMM' proof that a rail is healthy?
reflection.answer: Ripple, transients, current limit or noise may still violate operating requirements.

pages.title: Switch-mode conversion and energy storage
pages.text: Switch-mode regulators rapidly control a switch and transfer energy with inductors, capacitors, and sometimes transformers.
pages.remember: It transfers energy by switching and storage rather than dropping the full voltage difference continuously as heat.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Switch-mode regulators rapidly control a switch and transfer energy with inductors, capacitors, and sometimes transformers. Buck converters lower voltage; boost converters raise it. Ideal duty-cycle equations are teaching models, while real designs include diode/switch drops, losses, control and transient limits.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Switch nodes can generate damaging transients and EMI. Do not attach grounded probes to non-isolated primary circuits.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Switch-mode conversion and energy storage
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: For an ideal buck, 12 V input and 25% duty cycle suggest 3 V output.
Actual output changes with control method, operating mode, conduction and losses.
A boost example at D=0.5 has ideal Vout≈Vin/(1−0.5)=2Vin.
worked.conclusion: It transfers energy by switching and storage rather than dropping the full voltage difference continuously as heat.

reflection.ask: Why can a buck be more efficient than a linear regulator for large voltage reduction?
reflection.answer: It transfers energy by switching and storage rather than dropping the full voltage difference continuously as heat.

pages.title: Inductors, feedback, protection in switchers
pages.text: An inductor opposes abrupt current change, and an output capacitor resists abrupt voltage change.
pages.remember: It adjusts switching control to deliver more energy within its designed operating range.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

An inductor opposes abrupt current change, and an output capacitor resists abrupt voltage change. Feedback compares output with a reference and changes switching behavior to correct disturbances. Overcurrent, thermal and undervoltage protections can deliberately reduce or interrupt output.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Protection cycling can look like oscillation; distinguish commanded shutdown from unstable compensation. Only qualified personnel should diagnose line-powered SMPS internals.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Inductors, feedback, protection in switchers
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A converter intermittently shuts off when loaded.
Investigate protection threshold, load demand, input droop, thermal fault and output short before replacing the controller.
worked.conclusion: It adjusts switching control to deliver more energy within its designed operating range.

reflection.ask: What does a controller usually do when output falls below target but no protection limit is hit?
reflection.answer: It adjusts switching control to deliver more energy within its designed operating range.

pages.title: Ripple measurement and oscilloscope setup
pages.text: Ripple is a time-varying voltage superimposed on DC.
pages.remember: Probe-ground loop, coupling, bandwidth and acquisition settings can change observed waveform.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Ripple is a time-varying voltage superimposed on DC. Scope bandwidth, AC/DC coupling, probe attenuation, ground-loop geometry and noise pickup all affect the display. Short ground connections reduce unwanted inductive pickup when observing high-frequency ripple.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Never detach safety earth or attach a grounded scope lead to a hazardous non-isolated node. Scope setup is part of measurement evidence.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Ripple measurement and oscilloscope setup
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: If a rail is 5 V DC with 80 mV peak-to-peak ripple, a properly set scope can show the variations that a DMM may average away.
Record measurement bandwidth and probe configuration with the result.
worked.conclusion: Probe-ground loop, coupling, bandwidth and acquisition settings can change observed waveform.

reflection.ask: Why might two technicians measure different ripple on the same supply?
reflection.answer: Probe-ground loop, coupling, bandwidth and acquisition settings can change observed waveform.

pages.title: Batteries, current limits and protection
pages.text: A battery has nominal voltage but also internal resistance, chemistry-specific behavior, state-of-charge limits and fault energy.
pages.remember: Internal resistance and state of charge can cause large voltage sag under current demand.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A battery has nominal voltage but also internal resistance, chemistry-specific behavior, state-of-charge limits and fault energy. A current-limited bench supply is useful for controlled startup, yet its power/current settings require correct wiring and a risk assessment.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Lithium cells can present fire risk under shorts, puncture, incorrect charging or abuse. Use certified packs and approved training procedures.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Batteries, current limits and protection
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A source with 0.5 Ω internal resistance supplying 1 A loses about 0.5 V internally.
For a battery-backed device, include wiring and contact drops when measuring the voltage available to the load.
worked.conclusion: Internal resistance and state of charge can cause large voltage sag under current demand.

reflection.ask: Why can a battery read acceptable open-circuit voltage yet fail under load?
reflection.answer: Internal resistance and state of charge can cause large voltage sag under current demand.

pages.title: Power tree troubleshooting
pages.text: A power tree maps dependency: source, protection, intermediate rail, local regulator, and loads.
pages.remember: A regulator may be healthy but deliberately disabled by its control system.
pages.sourceLesson: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A power tree maps dependency: source, protection, intermediate rail, local regulator, and loads. Troubleshoot from a verified reference and known expected voltages; do not randomly swap parts. Correlate normal startup order, enable signals, load current, ripple and thermal behavior.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
A missing supply may be an intentional interlock; forced-enable tests can damage boards. Use paper/simulation unless a safe approved lab setup exists.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Power tree troubleshooting
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A 12 V input is present, 5 V rail absent and its regulator enable is 0 V.
Check the enable-control path before concluding the regulator itself is failed.
Document each expected and measured point with test condition.
worked.conclusion: A regulator may be healthy but deliberately disabled by its control system.

reflection.ask: Why does an enable-pin reading matter in a 'dead 5 V rail' diagnosis?
reflection.answer: A regulator may be healthy but deliberately disabled by its control system.

pages.title: Thermal budget and regulator selection
pages.text: Efficiency describes output power divided by input power.
pages.remember: Actual dissipated watts and the installation's thermal resistance may exceed safe junction temperature.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Efficiency describes output power divided by input power. A linear regulator dropping a large voltage under load may be unsuitable because heat scales with lost voltage × current. Thermal junction rise approximates dissipation × thermal resistance under specified conditions.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Datasheet θJA depends on PCB layout, airflow and package; it is not a universal resistor value.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Thermal budget and regulator selection
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Suppose 1.4 W regulator loss and θJA=50 °C/W; approximate junction rise is 70 °C above ambient in that test setup.
At 25 °C ambient it suggests about 95 °C junction before additional complications.
worked.conclusion: Actual dissipated watts and the installation's thermal resistance may exceed safe junction temperature.

reflection.ask: Why is a nominally 'rated' regulator still at risk of overheating?
reflection.answer: Actual dissipated watts and the installation's thermal resistance may exceed safe junction temperature.

pages.title: Power-supply acceptance checklist
pages.text: A supply is not accepted based on one isolated voltage number.
pages.remember: Specific source/load conditions, instrument setup, expected limits, observed results and pass/fail reasoning.
pages.sourceLesson: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A supply is not accepted based on one isolated voltage number. Record source condition, operating load, output DC level, ripple, startup, shutdown, current limit, protection and thermal observations. Separate results from paper predictions and physical measurements with provenance.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Do not manufacture results. If no safe bench hardware exists, present calculations and simulation as theoretical evidence only.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Power-supply acceptance checklist
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: For a 5 V rail, plan a table: no load, expected load, startup step, input-low condition and fault-protection condition.
For each, state predicted voltage/window, measurement method and accepted decision rule.
worked.conclusion: Specific source/load conditions, instrument setup, expected limits, observed results and pass/fail reasoning.

reflection.ask: What makes a power-supply test report reproducible?
reflection.answer: Specific source/load conditions, instrument setup, expected limits, observed results and pass/fail reasoning.

examples.title: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

detail.problem: A full-wave 100 Hz ripple supply provides 50 mA to a 1,000 µF capacitor. Estimate peak-to-peak ripple.
steps: ΔV ≈ 0.50 V peak-to-peak.
Treat this as a first estimate; diode conduction and ESR affect the measured waveform.
detail.answer: About 0.5 Vpp ripple.
detail.transfer: Doubling capacitance or ripple frequency halves the first-order ripple estimate.

examples.title: Power-supply blocks and their expected signals

detail.problem: A full-wave rectified 60 Hz supply uses 2200 uF and draws 0.20 A. Estimate capacitor ripple using deltaV≈I/(fC).
steps: Full-wave ripple frequency is approximately 120 Hz.
deltaV≈0.20/(120*0.0022)=0.758 V peak-to-peak approximate ripple.
The estimate ignores diode conduction angle, ESR, transformer regulation, and regulator behavior but gives useful scale.
detail.answer: Approximately 0.76 Vpp ripple at the reservoir capacitor in the simplified model.
detail.meaning: Ripple is a predictable function of load, capacitance, and recharge frequency, so a measured excess can guide diagnosis.

examples.title: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

detail.problem: A 3.3 V rail is correct with no load, drops to 2.4 V at 100 mA, and the bench supply remains in CV mode.
steps: The bench source is not current limiting.
Measure regulator input under load to check dropout/source path.
If input remains adequate, check regulator rating, thermal state, wiring resistance, and load current.
If input also falls, move upstream to source/rectifier/filter connections.
detail.answer: Use input-under-load to separate upstream collapse from regulator/load behavior.
detail.transfer: A two-node comparison provides more information than swapping the regulator immediately.

examples.title: Rail-by-rail bring-up and supply troubleshooting

detail.problem: A board has 12 V input, 5 V buck output, and 3.3 V LDO from the 5 V rail. Measurements: 12.1 V input, 5.0 V, 0.8 V at 3.3 V rail, LDO hot.
steps: The 12 V source and 5 V converter are likely functioning under this condition.
The 3.3 V LDO has adequate 5 V input but is hot with low output, suggesting overload/short, wrong orientation/part, or regulator fault/current limit.
Power down and measure 3.3 V rail resistance/inspect downstream loads before replacing the LDO.
If isolating a connector restores normal 3.3 V, move diagnosis into the disconnected load branch.
detail.answer: Focus on the 3.3 V regulator/load domain; the evidence does not support replacing the upstream 12-to-5 V converter.
detail.meaning: A power tree lets one measurement localize the failing domain.

examples.title: Junction behavior and semiconductor device roles

detail.problem: A 5 V supply drives a red LED approximated at 1.9 V with a 330 Ω resistor. Estimate current and resistor power.
steps: Resistor voltage = 5 − 1.9 = 3.1 V.
P resistor = I²R ≈ 0.029 W.
Verify the actual LED datasheet and current target; forward voltage is not exact.
detail.answer: About 9.4 mA and 29 mW in the resistor.
detail.transfer: This same load current becomes the minimum current the transistor switch must handle.

guided.text: Draw expected waveforms at transformer secondary, bridge output, reservoir capacitor, and regulated output.
For 100 mA load, 1000 uF, and 100 Hz ripple, estimate ripple voltage.
Compare a linear regulator and buck converter for efficiency, dissipation, noise, complexity, and required headroom.
Create a rail table for a board with 12 V input, 5 V, 3.3 V, and 1.2 V rails. Include source, load, tolerance, and one test point each.
A 3.3 V rail reads 3.30 V on a DMM but the MCU resets during radio transmit. State why the DMM result is insufficient and what scope capture you need.
List five stop conditions during first-power or rail-by-rail bring-up.

teachBack: Trace both a linear supply and a buck SMPS from input to regulated output. Explain what each major block does, what waveform you expect, and one fault symptom that points to that block.
Given a multi-rail embedded board, explain how you would use a power tree, current limit, DMM, and scope to find the first failing rail without changing multiple things at once.

questions.prompt: Why can an unplugged power supply remain hazardous?
choices: Unplugging always removes all stored energy instantly.
A disconnected supply cannot contain voltage.
Only its display can retain energy.
questions.explanation: Stored energy must be handled under the relevant safe procedure. These course labs use approved low-voltage sources, not mains repair.

questions.prompt: A full-wave rectifier is fed by 60 Hz AC. Before smoothing, how often do its output peaks repeat?
questions.explanation: Full-wave rectification uses both half-cycles, doubling the ripple frequency.

questions.prompt: In a basic rectifier supply, what does a reservoir capacitor do between charging peaks?
choices: Supplies load current while its voltage falls
Blocks all DC load current by definition
questions.explanation: Its stored energy supports the load between peaks. More load current or less capacitance generally increases ripple.

questions.prompt: What is a regulator intended to maintain within specified limits?
choices: Output voltage as input or load changes
The same temperature under every condition
questions.explanation: Regulation has operating limits, including input headroom, load capability and thermal constraints.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches a switch-mode power supply?
choices: It switches a power device and transfers energy through reactive components.
It relies only on a series resistor for all regulation.
It needs no feedback or control under any circumstances.
questions.explanation: Switching converters use controlled energy transfer. Filtering, regulation and layout still matter.

questions.prompt: A linear regulator drops 12 V to 5 V at 0.20 A. About how much power does it dissipate?
questions.explanation: Correct. (12−5) V × 0.20 A = 1.4 W, which requires thermal evaluation.

candidateQuestions.prompt: What distinguishes a supply with an isolating mains transformer from a non-isolated direct-line supply?
choices: Non-isolated supplies always output zero volts
The transformer design can provide galvanic isolation when correctly constructed
An isolation transformer eliminates every hazard
The two designs have identical isolation boundaries
candidateQuestions.explanation: An appropriately designed isolating transformer separates primary and secondary circuits galvanically; direct-line non-isolated designs can retain mains-referenced hazardous potentials.
candidateQuestions.origin: v3.0 unscored objective retrieval · provisional technical/editorial review

candidateQuestions.prompt: What is an advantage of a battery-backed low-voltage supply in a portable instrument?
choices: It requires a nearby AC outlet at all times
Its terminal voltage can never change
It can provide energy without an external mains connection during use
candidateQuestions.explanation: A battery stores chemical energy and can power a device away from an outlet. Voltage and available capacity depend on chemistry, load and state of charge.
candidateQuestions.origin: v3.0 unscored objective retrieval · provisional technical/editorial review

candidateQuestions.prompt: A classic C–L–C “pi” smoothing filter has which component sequence from input to output?
choices: Capacitor to common, series inductor, capacitor to common
candidateQuestions.explanation: A pi smoothing filter uses a shunt capacitor, series inductor and second shunt capacitor. It reduces ripple when designed for the load and applicable frequency.
candidateQuestions.origin: v3.0 unscored objective retrieval · provisional technical/editorial review

candidateQuestions.prompt: When studying integrated high-voltage transformer supplies, which statement is the safest and most technically appropriate?
choices: Recognize that compact transformer/switching assemblies can produce hazardous voltages and retain stored charge
Assume their output is safe after unplugging
Assume every integrated high-voltage design is isolated
Touch the output to verify it is de-energized
candidateQuestions.explanation: Integrated high-voltage assemblies may combine switching and transformation stages. Their isolation, output energy and stored-charge hazards must be assessed from authoritative device documentation.
candidateQuestions.origin: v3.0 unscored objective retrieval · provisional technical/editorial review

candidateQuestions.prompt: A fuse has opened in an equipment power-input path. Which replacement decision is correct?
choices: Replace it with a larger current rating to prevent nuisance trips
Use the specified fuse type and current, voltage and interrupting ratings after investigating the cause
Use a wire jumper to diagnose faults routinely
Select a replacement by color alone
candidateQuestions.explanation: Protective devices must match the specified application characteristics, including current, voltage, interrupting capacity and time response. Repeated opening is a fault symptom.

pages.title: An amplifier transfers supply energy to a signal
pages.text: An amplifier reproduces an input's information at an output with a different available voltage, current or power, using energy from its DC supply.
pages.remember: It draws the additional energy from its power supplies.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

An amplifier reproduces an input's information at an output with a different available voltage, current or power, using energy from its DC supply. Gain is a ratio between defined quantities and test points, not 'output volts' alone. Amplifiers can be configured for voltage, current or power gain with tradeoffs.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Gain cannot be evaluated properly without input reference, load, frequency and operating conditions.

worked.heading: Reason it through · An amplifier transfers supply energy to a signal
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A sinusoidal input of 0.2 V peak produces 1.0 V peak at the same stated load.
Voltage gain magnitude is 1/0.2=5 V/V.
Compare both signals' phase and ensure output rails allow that amplitude.
worked.conclusion: It draws the additional energy from its power supplies.

reflection.ask: How can an amplifier deliver greater output energy than its input signal carries?
reflection.answer: It draws the additional energy from its power supplies.

pages.title: Decibels and voltage gain
pages.text: Decibels express logarithmic ratios.
pages.remember: Approximately 6.02 dB, with phase described separately.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Decibels express logarithmic ratios. Power ratios use 10 log10(Pout/Pin). For voltage ratios under the appropriate equal-impedance or gain interpretation, use 20 log10|Vout/Vin|. A negative voltage gain indicates inversion, while magnitude in dB does not by itself encode phase.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Do not apply 20 log10 to a power ratio or use an amplifier dB reading without defining units and impedances.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Decibels and voltage gain
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: If |Av|=10, gain=20 dB.
If power doubles, 10 log10(2)≈3.01 dB.
If |Av|=0.5, gain=20 log10(0.5)≈−6.02 dB (attenuation).
worked.conclusion: Approximately 6.02 dB, with phase described separately.

reflection.ask: What is the voltage gain in dB for magnitude ratio 2?
reflection.answer: Approximately 6.02 dB, with phase described separately.

pages.title: Signal levels, loading and impedance
pages.text: Sources have finite output impedance, and amplifier inputs draw some current.
pages.remember: The real input was attenuated by source/loading before amplification.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Sources have finite output impedance, and amplifier inputs draw some current. Loading forms a divider and can alter signal amplitude before any amplification. Output impedance and the attached load affect final waveform and available current. High input impedance is often desired for voltage measurement or buffering.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
High input impedance is not always the universal design goal; power and RF systems may intentionally match impedance.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Signal levels, loading and impedance
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A 1 V source with 1 kΩ source resistance driving a 1 kΩ input delivers 0.5 V to the input.
Replacing it with a 100 kΩ input delivers about 0.990 V, before later stage gain.
worked.conclusion: The real input was attenuated by source/loading before amplification.

reflection.ask: Why can a perfect mathematical gain stage still produce an unexpectedly low measured output?
reflection.answer: The real input was attenuated by source/loading before amplification.

pages.title: Common-emitter and common-source signal inversion
pages.text: Increasing BJT base drive raises collector current.
pages.remember: More current means more drop across the collector resistor and less node voltage.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Increasing BJT base drive raises collector current. Across a collector resistor, larger current creates more voltage drop, lowering collector voltage. That explains the usual 180-degree small-signal inversion of common-emitter stages. Common-source FET stages behave analogously under suitable bias.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
The statement applies in the intended linear operation region, not when the transistor is off or saturated.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Common-emitter and common-source signal inversion
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: At one instant, input rises slightly; collector current rises; collector resistor drop rises; collector voltage falls.
Sketch input and output polarities to establish inversion without merely memorizing the label.
worked.conclusion: More current means more drop across the collector resistor and less node voltage.

reflection.ask: Why is a collector-resistor output often inverted relative to the input?
reflection.answer: More current means more drop across the collector resistor and less node voltage.

pages.title: Amplifier classes and efficiency tradeoffs
pages.text: Class A conducts across the full signal cycle and is simple but inefficient; Class B output devices each cover about half a cycle and can show crossover distortion; Class AB biases around the crossover to reduce that artifact.
pages.remember: Its output devices need bias to hand off conduction; inadequate bias creates crossover dead-zone distortion.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Class A conducts across the full signal cycle and is simple but inefficient; Class B output devices each cover about half a cycle and can show crossover distortion; Class AB biases around the crossover to reduce that artifact. Class D uses high-frequency switching and output filtering, distinct from a linear Class A/B path.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Class designation says nothing about guaranteed sound quality or safety by itself. Read a particular topology and device specification.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Amplifier classes and efficiency tradeoffs
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Compare a sinewave output with a small notch around zero (possible crossover distortion) against flat-topped clipping at peaks (rail or overload limitation).
They indicate different root causes and repair paths.
worked.conclusion: Its output devices need bias to hand off conduction; inadequate bias creates crossover dead-zone distortion.

reflection.ask: Why does a Class B push-pull stage sometimes produce a small notch near zero crossing?
reflection.answer: Its output devices need bias to hand off conduction; inadequate bias creates crossover dead-zone distortion.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use written or simulated cases only for hazardous mains supplies, stored-energy power circuitry and high-energy thyristor/IGBT systems. Physical testing requires controlled conditions.

pages.title: Op-amp inputs, supplies and open-loop action
pages.text: An operational amplifier amplifies the differential input V+−V− with very high open-loop gain and output limitations.
pages.remember: Huge open-loop gain drives output toward a rail for tiny differential error.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

An operational amplifier amplifies the differential input V+−V− with very high open-loop gain and output limitations. External negative feedback controls stable closed-loop gain in most linear applications. The plus/minus symbols identify non-inverting/inverting inputs, not the supply rails.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
No real output reaches beyond its supplies. Common-mode input range and output swing ratings can constrain it well before rails.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Op-amp inputs, supplies and open-loop action
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Supply an op amp on ±5 V rails; if positive input is slightly greater than negative input and no suitable feedback holds linear operation, output tends toward the positive swing limit rather than 'the tiny difference' itself.
worked.conclusion: Huge open-loop gain drives output toward a rail for tiny differential error.

reflection.ask: Why is an op amp without negative feedback usually poor as a linear 5× amplifier?
reflection.answer: Huge open-loop gain drives output toward a rail for tiny differential error.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use written or simulated cases only for hazardous mains supplies, stored-energy power circuitry and high-energy thyristor/IGBT systems. Physical testing requires controlled conditions.

pages.title: Inverting amplifier calculation
pages.text: The inverting configuration sends input through Rin to the inverting node and feeds output through Rf; the non-inverting input is at the circuit's reference.
pages.remember: Output polarity is inverted relative to the defined input reference.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

The inverting configuration sends input through Rin to the inverting node and feeds output through Rf; the non-inverting input is at the circuit's reference. With valid negative feedback and linear operation, ideal gain is −Rf/Rin. The inverting node is an approximate virtual reference, not physically shorted to ground.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
If output clips or input goes outside allowed common-mode range, the ideal inverting equation is invalid.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Inverting amplifier calculation
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Rin=10 kΩ, Rf=47 kΩ and Vin=+0.20 V give Vout≈−4.7×0.20=−0.94 V, provided rails and bandwidth allow it.
The input current through Rin approximately matches feedback current.
worked.conclusion: Output polarity is inverted relative to the defined input reference.

reflection.ask: What does the minus sign in −Rf/Rin signify?
reflection.answer: Output polarity is inverted relative to the defined input reference.

pages.title: Non-inverting gain and follower
pages.text: Non-inverting configuration applies signal to plus input and uses feedback divider at minus input.
pages.remember: It provides isolation with high input impedance and stronger output drive.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Non-inverting configuration applies signal to plus input and uses feedback divider at minus input. Under ideal negative feedback assumptions, closed-loop gain is 1+Rf/Rg. A follower connects output to the inverting input, yielding approximately unity voltage gain and improved drive/isolation.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Some single-supply op amps cannot sense or output near either rail; 'rail-to-rail' must specify input and/or output explicitly.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Non-inverting gain and follower
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Rf=40 kΩ and Rg=10 kΩ give gain≈5.
A 0.2 V input predicts 1.0 V output if supply headroom and load allow it.
Check whether the op amp supports input range near ground.
worked.conclusion: It provides isolation with high input impedance and stronger output drive.

reflection.ask: Why is a unity follower useful despite having 1× voltage gain?
reflection.answer: It provides isolation with high input impedance and stronger output drive.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use written or simulated cases only for hazardous mains supplies, stored-energy power circuitry and high-energy thyristor/IGBT systems. Physical testing requires controlled conditions.

pages.title: Feedback modifies gain, bandwidth and stability
pages.text: Negative feedback reduces sensitivity to uncertain open-loop gain, but closed-loop frequency response, compensation and phase margin determine stability.
pages.remember: High open-loop gain drives the feedback node to closely follow the reference within valid operating range.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Negative feedback reduces sensitivity to uncertain open-loop gain, but closed-loop frequency response, compensation and phase margin determine stability. The common ideal 'V+=V−' approximation holds only when negative feedback is operating and output remains linear. Excess delay can make a supposedly negative-feedback loop oscillate.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Feedback may also change input/output impedance and noise. Compensation requirements depend on specific device and load.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Feedback modifies gain, bandwidth and stability
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: An op amp has open-loop gain 100,000 at low frequency, but a resistor network commands closed-loop gain 10.
The loop uses output corrections to keep differential input tiny; do not manually multiply input by 100,000 as final closed-loop output.
worked.conclusion: High open-loop gain drives the feedback node to closely follow the reference within valid operating range.

reflection.ask: Why can negative feedback produce predictable gain from simple resistors?
reflection.answer: High open-loop gain drives the feedback node to closely follow the reference within valid operating range.

pages.title: Bandwidth and gain-bandwidth product
pages.text: Amplifier gain is not constant at all frequencies.
pages.remember: Finite closed-loop bandwidth reduces gain and adds phase shift as frequency rises.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Amplifier gain is not constant at all frequencies. Many compensated voltage-feedback op amps have an approximately constant gain-bandwidth product over a range, so high closed-loop gain trades against small-signal bandwidth. Slew rate limits large-signal fast changes independently of small-signal bandwidth.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
The estimate does not substitute for checking stability, slew rate, output current or datasheet plots.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Bandwidth and gain-bandwidth product
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: For a 1 MHz unity-gain-bandwidth amplifier, a closed-loop gain of 10 suggests bandwidth around 100 kHz in a simple one-pole model.
This is an estimate: load and actual device data can change it.
worked.conclusion: Finite closed-loop bandwidth reduces gain and adds phase shift as frequency rises.

reflection.ask: Why can a circuit pass a 1 kHz gain test but fail at 200 kHz?
reflection.answer: Finite closed-loop bandwidth reduces gain and adds phase shift as frequency rises.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use written or simulated cases only for hazardous mains supplies, stored-energy power circuitry and high-energy thyristor/IGBT systems. Physical testing requires controlled conditions.

pages.title: Clipping, slew limiting and distortion
pages.text: Flat output peaks commonly indicate clipping at a supply/output limit or current constraint.
pages.remember: The output cannot change as quickly as the demanded waveform requires.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Flat output peaks commonly indicate clipping at a supply/output limit or current constraint. Slew-rate limiting creates slope-limited waveforms even if small-signal frequency response seems sufficient. Distortion results can depend on input amplitude, frequency, load, feedback and bias.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Do not confuse a clipped waveform with a probe set incorrectly or with a deliberately limited output. Record setup before interpreting shape.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Clipping, slew limiting and distortion
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: For 2 V peak sine at 100 kHz, maximum slope is 2πfVpk≈1.26 V/µs.
A 0.5 V/µs op amp cannot reproduce it faithfully even if a low-frequency gain test passes.
worked.conclusion: The output cannot change as quickly as the demanded waveform requires.

reflection.ask: What does slew-rate limiting reveal?
reflection.answer: The output cannot change as quickly as the demanded waveform requires.

pages.title: Measuring gain without fooling yourself
pages.text: Use the same RMS or peak convention at input and output, verify probe attenuation, channel reference, and load, and compare frequency at defined points.
pages.remember: Input/output measurement conventions, frequency, load, supply, and instrument/probe configuration.
pages.sourceLesson: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Use the same RMS or peak convention at input and output, verify probe attenuation, channel reference, and load, and compare frequency at defined points. If output phase inverts, still calculate magnitude gain from ratios and state inversion separately. Measure DC offset if it alters headroom.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
A DMM may not accurately read non-sinusoidal or higher-frequency AC unless its bandwidth and true-RMS spec fit the signal.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Measuring gain without fooling yourself
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Input 200 mV rms and output 1.00 V rms gives gain=5 V/V≈13.98 dB; note whether output is inverted and record frequency/load.
A 10× probe misconfiguration can fake a huge gain.
worked.conclusion: Input/output measurement conventions, frequency, load, supply, and instrument/probe configuration.

reflection.ask: What conditions belong beside a published amplifier gain measurement?
reflection.answer: Input/output measurement conventions, frequency, load, supply, and instrument/probe configuration.

pages.title: Amplifier fault isolation by waveform signature
pages.text: Compare expected waveforms stage by stage, starting with input and power rails.
pages.remember: It omits waveform shape, amplitude, load, frequency, bias and power-rail conditions.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Compare expected waveforms stage by stage, starting with input and power rails. Saturated bias, missing feedback, wrong reference, failed output stage, current limiting and open coupling capacitors each leave different evidence. Test the simplest plausible cause with a non-destructive measurement before component replacement.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
This is an educational low-voltage paper/simulation diagnosis, not permission to probe hazardous equipment.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Amplifier fault isolation by waveform signature
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: A sinewave input is correct but output has a flat upper peak.
Inspect output rail headroom and DC bias; check load current before swapping feedback resistors.
If both peaks distort symmetrically only at high frequency, evaluate slew rate and bandwidth.
worked.conclusion: It omits waveform shape, amplitude, load, frequency, bias and power-rail conditions.

reflection.ask: Why is 'the output has distortion' too weak to diagnose a specific failure?
reflection.answer: It omits waveform shape, amplitude, load, frequency, bias and power-rail conditions.

goldTeaching.sectionNote: Use written or simulated cases only for hazardous mains supplies, stored-energy power circuitry and high-energy thyristor/IGBT systems. Physical testing requires controlled conditions.

pages.title: Amplifier design-review case
pages.text: Combine gain equations, rails, input range, output load, bandwidth, slew rate and thermal limits.
pages.remember: Verified device limits, a documented circuit, expected calculations and appropriately captured or simulated waveforms.
pages.sourceLesson: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Combine gain equations, rails, input range, output load, bandwidth, slew rate and thermal limits. A technically credible result states conditions and uncertainty rather than presenting one ideal formula as a guaranteed behavior.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
A mathematically valid gain resistor pair is not enough to select a physical device.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Amplifier design-review case
worked.scenario: Work the following specific example before comparing your own steps.
steps: Specify an amplifier for 0.2 V peak input, desired 1 V peak output at 5 kHz.
Gain=5; minimum sine slew≈2π×5000×1≈0.0314 V/µs; verify actual op amp gain-bandwidth, headroom, common-mode range and output current from datasheet.
worked.conclusion: Verified device limits, a documented circuit, expected calculations and appropriately captured or simulated waveforms.

reflection.ask: What evidence would justify saying the proposed amplifier meets requirements?
reflection.answer: Verified device limits, a documented circuit, expected calculations and appropriately captured or simulated waveforms.

examples.title: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

detail.problem: An inverting op-amp uses Rin = 10 kΩ, Rf = 47 kΩ, and Vin = 0.20 V. Find ideal output.
steps: Check whether the supply rails and input common-mode permit this result.
Check load and bandwidth before expecting the ideal value physically.
detail.answer: Ideal Vout = −0.94 V.
detail.transfer: If powered from a single 0–5 V supply with no bias, a negative output request will clip near the lower rail.

examples.title: Gain, dB, feedback, and ideal op-amp rules

detail.problem: A non-inverting op-amp uses Rg=10 kOhm and Rf=40 kOhm with Vin=0.4 V. Supply is 0-5 V and the op-amp can swing only to about 0.2-4.8 V.
steps: Ideal gain=1+40k/10k=5.
Ideal output=0.4*5=2.0 V, inside the stated output range.
If Vin rises to 1.2 V, ideal output would be 6 V, impossible on a 5 V supply.
The real output saturates near its upper swing limit; the virtual-input-equality assumption no longer supports the linear gain equation.
detail.answer: 2.0 V is plausible for 0.4 V input; 6 V is not, so a 1.2 V input would drive the stage into saturation.
detail.meaning: Closed-loop formulas must be checked against supply and operating limits.

examples.title: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

detail.problem: A non-inverting stage designed for gain 11 produces the correct low-frequency output, but gain falls and the waveform becomes triangular at high frequency.
steps: Correct low-frequency gain makes resistor ratio/feedback topology plausible.
High-frequency gain loss suggests finite bandwidth.
Triangular output at large amplitude suggests slew-rate limiting.
Reduce amplitude and compare; check datasheet gain-bandwidth and slew rate.
detail.answer: Prioritize bandwidth/slew limitations rather than resistor replacement.
detail.transfer: Changing one condition—amplitude—separates small-signal bandwidth from large-signal slew behavior.

examples.title: Measure and troubleshoot a signal chain

detail.problem: A non-inverting stage should have gain 5. It measures gain 5 at 1 kHz and 100 mV input, but at 100 kHz and 1 V input the output becomes triangular with much lower amplitude.
steps: The low-frequency result supports the resistor ratio and feedback polarity.
High frequency plus large output swing increases required slew rate.
Estimate required sine-wave slew rate 2*pi*f*Vpk and compare with datasheet.
Reduce input amplitude at 100 kHz. If shape improves, slew-rate limitation is supported; if gain remains low, also check gain-bandwidth.
detail.answer: Prioritize slew-rate and bandwidth limits rather than replacing feedback resistors.
detail.meaning: Changing amplitude while holding frequency separates large-signal slew behavior from small-signal bandwidth.

guided.text: Calculate gain for an inverting stage Rin=10 kOhm, Rf=47 kOhm and predict output for +0.2 V input.
For a BJT stage, explain why measuring collector at nearly the supply rail can suggest cutoff while near emitter voltage can suggest saturation, depending on topology.
A stage has correct low-frequency gain but rolls off early. List gain-bandwidth, coupling capacitors, source/load impedance, and probe loading as separate hypotheses.
Create a signal budget for a two-stage chain: sensor 100 mVpp -> gain 10 -> gain 2 -> ADC max 3.3 Vpp. Identify headroom risk.
A stage output is correct unloaded but drops 40% with a 1 kOhm load. Calculate approximate output current and compare it with the device's drive rating.
For a railed op-amp output, list checks in order: supplies, input/common-mode, feedback continuity/polarity, expected gain, output load.

pages.title: Workshop safety and ESD are separate protections
pages.text: Electrostatic discharge can harm sensitive semiconductors without a noticeable shock.
pages.remember: ESD primarily protects components; ventilation, heat, lead handling and electrical isolation protect people and environment.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Electrostatic discharge can harm sensitive semiconductors without a noticeable shock. ESD-controlled benches use verified dissipative surfaces, grounded equipment, qualified personnel grounding, and suitable packaging. Electrical shock and thermal burns remain separate hazards; an ESD wrist strap is never used to make hazardous energized work safe.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Always follow workplace ESD plans and safety procedures; merely owning an antistatic mat does not prove it is properly grounded.

pages.text: A printed circuit board carries copper traces, pads, plated through-holes, vias, solder mask and component identifiers.

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A printed circuit board carries copper traces, pads, plated through-holes, vias, solder mask and component identifiers. Through-hole component leads go through drilled pads; surface-mount parts rest on solderable land patterns. A board can have several layers and planes, so visual traces alone do not reveal every connection.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Do not gouge solder mask or infer hidden copper from a top-side photo. Use board documentation if available.

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Solder alloys differ in melting range, metallurgy and reliability behavior. Leaded and lead-free processes have different process windows and required workplace controls. Flux supports oxide removal and wetting but does not replace solder joint design or adequate thermal transfer.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Do not recommend random higher temperatures to fix every joint. Excessive heat can damage pads and components.

pages.title: Heat flow, iron tips and thermal recovery
pages.text: A soldering iron transfers heat into the joint through the wetted contact area and tip mass; temperature setting alone is not the heat delivered.
pages.remember: Better contact and heat transfer can reduce total dwell time.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A soldering iron transfers heat into the joint through the wetted contact area and tip mass; temperature setting alone is not the heat delivered. A correctly sized clean tinned tip can heat both lead and pad more efficiently than a tiny oxidized tip. Large copper planes draw away heat.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
The correct temperature is process- and equipment-specific; avoid setting values without manufacturer and alloy guidance.

worked.conclusion: Better contact and heat transfer can reduce total dwell time.

reflection.ask: Why can a slightly larger clean tip be less damaging than a tiny overheated tip?

pages.title: Flux and solder wetting
pages.text: For solder to form a sound metallic bond, molten solder must wet clean component metallization and pad copper/tin finishes.
pages.remember: The underlying wetting, temperature and cleanliness problem remains.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

For solder to form a sound metallic bond, molten solder must wet clean component metallization and pad copper/tin finishes. Oxides, oils, insufficient heating and wrong flux can prevent spreading. Solder beads that sit on a surface are not equivalent to a wetted fillet.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Visual shape alone does not certify high-reliability workmanship; use the applicable organization's acceptability criteria.

pages.title: Cold joints, bridges and lifted pads
pages.text: A poor solder joint may result from disturbed cooling, inadequate wetting, cracks or incomplete heat transfer; a solder bridge connects nodes that should be separate.
pages.remember: Optical appearance alone does not establish correct wetting, internal fill, mechanical security or electrical behavior.

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A poor solder joint may result from disturbed cooling, inadequate wetting, cracks or incomplete heat transfer; a solder bridge connects nodes that should be separate. Pads can lift after mechanical force, repeated heat or unsuitable rework technique. Appearance, x-ray or electrical tests may all be needed for some assemblies.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
A shiny joint is not always good and a matte lead-free finish is not necessarily bad. Workmanship acceptability is controlled by a defined standard.

pages.title: Desoldering wick and suction
pages.text: Desoldering removes solder while trying to preserve pads, plated holes and component leads.
pages.remember: The mechanical force can tear copper plating and pads from the board.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Desoldering removes solder while trying to preserve pads, plated holes and component leads. Fluxed copper braid draws molten solder by capillarity; a vacuum tool can remove molten solder, especially from through-hole joints. The method must match board thermal mass and package type.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Mechanical force on a partially soldered lead can rip out plating. Allow cooling and reassess before repeated heating cycles.

pages.title: Rework heat budget and thermal damage
pages.text: Every rework cycle exposes pads, laminate, adhesive and components to thermal stress.
pages.remember: Cumulative thermal exposure and mechanical stress can weaken copper adhesion and nearby parts.
pages.sourceLesson: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Every rework cycle exposes pads, laminate, adhesive and components to thermal stress. Use the manufacturer's profile and suitable preheat/tip/nozzle methods for the package; observe limits on repeat cycles. If a pad has lifted or a trace is torn, changing the component may not restore the circuit.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
BGA and high-density work can require controlled stations, fixtures, x-ray and specialized qualification. DIY heat guns are not a substitute.

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

SMT components often lack visible leads; part size, package marking, pin-one indicators and polarity can be hard to see. Package drawings and assembly instructions are more reliable than guessing from a similar part. Solder paste and reflow use controlled process variables; hand repair depends on package accessibility.
Where the model breaks or a technician can be misled
Some diode body bands and board silk conventions differ; documentation wins over a generalized visual rule.

examples.title: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

detail.problem: A through-hole joint forms a dull ball around the lead and does not spread over the pad.
steps: This suggests inadequate wetting, contamination, insufficient heat transfer, or movement.
Inspect tip condition, surface cleanliness, flux, temperature, and whether pad and lead were heated together.
Reflow with controlled heat only if the pad is intact and the process is safe.
Inspect, continuity-check, and functionally verify afterward.
detail.answer: Treat the shape as evidence of poor wetting; correct the process, then verify electrically.
detail.transfer: The same diagnostic habit separates symptom from cause in electronics faults.

examples.title: ESD control and solder/rework fundamentals

detail.problem: A through-hole joint looks dull and has a ring-like boundary around the lead. Continuity is intermittent when the board is flexed slightly.
steps: The symptom supports a mechanically/electrically unreliable joint rather than appearance alone.
Power down and inspect under magnification for incomplete wetting, cracking, contamination, or pad damage.
If rework is appropriate, use flux and controlled heat to fully reflow the joint rather than adding a large solder blob.
After cooling/cleaning, inspect geometry and verify continuity with gentle mechanical stability—without stressing the board.
detail.answer: Treat it as a suspect disturbed/cold or cracked joint, rework with controlled process if permitted, then visually and electrically verify.
detail.meaning: Workmanship acceptance combines observation, process, and verification; shine alone is not a criterion.

examples.title: Make physical changes traceable with Git and lab records

detail.problem: A firmware change and wire rework are both made before a failed test begins passing.
steps: Two variables changed, so root cause is not established.
Record both changes and restore/test one at a time if safe.
Create separate commits/notes for firmware and physical rework.
Repeat the original test and adjacent regression tests at a named revision.
detail.answer: Separate changes and bind verification evidence to an exact hardware/software configuration.
detail.transfer: This is essential when an R&D technician and engineer collaborate across revisions.

examples.title: Make physical changes traceable with Git and lab records

detail.problem: A connector pin is re-crimped after intermittent continuity. The circuit now passes, but there is no record of the original fault or tool/die used.
steps: The passing result is useful but not reproducible evidence of workmanship quality.
Record connector/terminal/wire identity, observed original failure, crimp tool/die setting if available, before/after inspection, pull/continuity evidence, and final test.
Link the record to the correct board/harness revision and any related test script revision.
If using Git, commit the note/test update without credentials or unrelated generated files.
detail.answer: Add configuration, procedure, evidence, and traceability so another technician can understand and reproduce the repair.
detail.meaning: Traceability turns a one-time fix into engineering evidence.

examples.title: Retention: workmanship, cabling, measurement, and safety

detail.problem: After header rework, continuity is correct but the board intermittently resets when the cable moves.
steps: Static continuity does not rule out weak joint, pin retention, strain, or supply dip.
Inspect under magnification and monitor relevant rail/reset while applying only safe controlled movement.
Separate harness, connector, and board joint by substitution or boundary measurement.
Repair confirmed cause; repeat static, movement, and functional tests.
detail.answer: Use mechanical plus time-domain electrical evidence; do not accept continuity alone.
detail.transfer: The case becomes a strong portfolio story when documented honestly from symptom to retest.

guided.text: List the purpose of flux, correct heat transfer, solder wick, magnification, and ESD controls in a rework operation.
Classify three cases: solder bridge between adjacent pads, lifted pad after overheating, and insufficient wetting around a lead. For each, name the likely risk and a safe next action.
Explain why a random jumper wire may be unacceptable for a damaged high-speed PCB trace even if continuity is restored.
Write a good commit message and lab-note entry for replacing a 10 kOhm resistor with the correct 1 kOhm value after diagnosing a divider error.
Given a folder containing source code, oscilloscope PNGs, a password file, build outputs, and a test report, decide what belongs in version control and what should be excluded or handled differently.
Rewrite the sentence 'the solder joint was bad so I fixed it' into observation, interpretation, corrective action, and verification.

teachBack: Explain what creates a reliable solder joint, why solder wick works, what makes BGA/pad repair different from simple through-hole rework, and why ESD/physical-skill claims require real procedures and evidence.

Explain how you would document a real hardware rework so a second technician can reconstruct what was wrong, what changed, what tools/materials were used, and why the final verification is trustworthy. Include Git's role and its limits.
Explain how you would verify a solder or harness repair using both workmanship criteria and electrical evidence, and clearly state what simulation can and cannot prove.

pages.title: Place value: one quantity, different bases
pages.text: A numeral is a compact description of how many units of each positional weight are present.
pages.remember: Each binary digit contributes its position weight when it is one: 32, 8, 4 and 1 total 45.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

A numeral is a compact description of how many units of each positional weight are present. In base ten, the positions are powers of ten; base two uses 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. The rightmost position is weight one. An electrical circuit stores bits as two defined voltage ranges, but the value is a mathematical interpretation of those bits, not a new kind of electricity.
Where this model can mislead you
A leading zero changes display width but not unsigned magnitude. A bit string may instead be a signed quantity or a control code; interpretation always depends on representation and bit width.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Place value: one quantity, different bases
worked.scenario: Predict the result before reading each reasoned step.
steps: Expand binary 101101₂ from right to left: 1×32 + 0×16 + 1×8 + 1×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = 45₁₀.
Verify by recombining 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 rather than by memorizing a conversion table.
Reverse the calculation by repeatedly selecting the largest power of two that fits 45.
worked.conclusion: Each binary digit contributes its position weight when it is one: 32, 8, 4 and 1 total 45.

reflection.ask: Explain, without using a calculator, why 101101₂ equals 45₁₀.
reflection.answer: Each binary digit contributes its position weight when it is one: 32, 8, 4 and 1 total 45.

pages.title: Binary, octal and hexadecimal grouping
pages.text: Hexadecimal and octal are notation conveniences for digital engineers.
pages.remember: Four; sixteen possible combinations are represented by 2⁴ bit patterns.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Hexadecimal and octal are notation conveniences for digital engineers. One hex digit encodes exactly four bits because 16=2⁴; one octal digit encodes three bits because 8=2³. Group bits from the right for whole numbers and pad the left with zeros when necessary. A–F are values ten through fifteen, not six extra wires.
Where this model can mislead you
Do not treat hexadecimal characters as decimal digits when doing arithmetic. When converting fractions, grouping and padding occur on the opposite side of the radix point.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Binary, octal and hexadecimal grouping
worked.scenario: Predict the result before reading each reasoned step.
steps: Convert 11010110₂ to hexadecimal by grouping 1101 0110 → D6₁₆.
Convert 101101₂ to octal as 101 101 → 55₈.
Check D6₁₆ as 13×16 + 6 = 214₁₀.
If someone wrote 0xD6, the prefix signals hexadecimal notation, not a different value.
worked.conclusion: Four; sixteen possible combinations are represented by 2⁴ bit patterns.

reflection.ask: How many binary digits correspond to one hex digit, and why?
reflection.answer: Four; sixteen possible combinations are represented by 2⁴ bit patterns.

pages.title: Boolean variables and the electrical abstraction
pages.text: Boolean algebra deals with two logical conditions, false and true.
pages.remember: AND; F=HOT·ENABLE, because a zero on either input prevents the true output.
pages.sourceLesson: Binary, hexadecimal, gates, and sequential state

paragraphs: The physical model and meaning

Boolean algebra deals with two logical conditions, false and true. Logic gates are physical circuits that map input voltage ranges to those states, subject to threshold specifications. AND means both conditions must be true; OR permits either; NOT reverses a condition. The mathematical symbols describe relationships, not arbitrary output voltages.
Where this model can mislead you

Never assume a logic HIGH is exactly 5 V. Each logic family specifies input limits, output guarantees and supply range. Using the correct Boolean equation does not fix an incompatible physical interface.

worked.heading: Reason it through · Boolean variables and the electrical abstraction
worked.scenario: Predict the result before reading each reasoned step.
steps: For a cooling fan controlled by HOT and ENABLE, define F=HOT·ENABLE.
Now contrast the expression HOT+ENABLE, where '+' is OR, not numerical addition.
Use this truth table to explain which behavior the machine needs.
worked.conclusion: AND; F=HOT·ENABLE, because a zero on either input prevents the true output.

reflection.ask: A fan should run only when both HOT and ENABLE are true. Which operation models this?
reflection.answer: AND; F=HOT·ENABLE, because a zero on either input prevents the true output.
